item.title: The Giants just traded for J.J. McCarthy. Will he start for them?
item.description: The Giants acquired J.J. McCarthy in a trade from the Vikings. Will he start for New York, or will Jameis Winston continue to hold onto that role?
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants are trading for Minnesota Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy just one week after losing their starter, Jaxson Dart, for the season because of a knee injury.

The Giants sent a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Vikings to land McCarthy, a first-round pick from the 2024 NFL Draft who had fallen out of favor after two-plus seasons in Minnesota.

McCarthy missed his entire rookie season because of a knee injury before being named the Vikings' starting quarterback for the 2025 campaign. He struggled across 10 starts that season, posting a 6-4 record but completing just 57.6% of his passes for 1,632 yards, 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions.

McCarthy spent the 2026 NFL offseason competing with Kyler Murray for the Vikings' starting job. The job was ultimately handed to Murray before Week 1 of the preseason; meanwhile, McCarthy ended up losing the backup job to veteran Carson Wentz and began the season as the Vikings' emergency third-string quarterback.

Now, McCarthy will join John Harbaugh – brother of McCarthy's college coach at Michigan, Jim Harbaugh – in the hopes that a change of scenery can restore some of the prospect shine that dulled across his tenure with the Vikings.

But what opportunities will McCarthy be given to prove himself? Here's how the Giants are planning to use the 23-year-old after acquiring him via trade.

Will J.J. McCarthy start for the Giants?

McCarthy isn't expected to be immediately elevated into the Giants' starting quarterback job after being acquired via trade from the Vikings.

Harbaugh indicated during his postgame news conference following New York's 12-7 win over the Tennessee Titans in Week 3 that the team was planning to keep veteran Jameis Winston entrenched as its starting quarterback regardless of how it addressed the position.

"Yes. Yes, I do," Harbaugh told reporters when asked whether he believed Winston would be the team's starter moving forward. "Yes, I do."

Harbaugh also made it clear that Winston's performance against the Titans would " not at all" impact his status as the team's starting quarterback.

"The plans are the plans," Harbaugh said. "The opportunities that you have are the opportunities you have. No matter what, we're going to do everything we can to make our team as strong as we can based on what options we have."

Winston, 32, is a 12-year NFL veteran who was selected No. 1 overall by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in the 2015 NFL Draft. He has a career record of 37-53 across 90 starts and has completed 60.9% of his passes for 25,021 yards, 156 touchdowns and 114 interceptions.

Winston is known for having a gunslinger's mentality, which caused him to endure turnover issues during his time as a starter. He is the lone quarterback in NFL history to record at least 30 touchdowns and 30 interceptions in a single season – a feat he achieved with the Buccaneers in 2019 – but is also one of just nine different NFL quarterbacks to record at least 5,000 passing yards in a season.

If Winston's turnover issues flare up, that could afford McCarthy a chance to usurp the starting role from the veteran. For now, though, Harbaugh seems content to trust Winston, who signed a two-year extension on eve of the 2026 campaign to keep him tethered to New York through the 2028 NFL season.

Giants QB depth chart

McCarthy seems likely to slot in as the Giants' top backup quarterback after being acquired from the Vikings. Below is a look at the pecking order within the room with Dart out of action.

  1. Jameis Winston
  2. J.J. McCarthy
  3. Jake Haener

Haener, a 2023 fourth-round pick by the New Orleans Saints, began the season on the Giants' practice squad as their third-string quarterback. He was signed to the active roster ahead of Week 3 and served as Winston's backup against the Titans.

Haener – who has an 0-1 record in one career start and has completed 46.2% of his career passes for 226 yards, one touchdown and one interception – figures to revert to his third-string role with McCarthy in tow. However, he may remain the backup short-term as McCarthy acclimates to the Giants' Matt Nagy and Greg Roman-led offense.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: The Giants just traded for J.J. McCarthy. Will he start for them?

item.title: NFL news, live updates: Giants trade for J.J. McCarthy following season-ending injury to Jaxson Dart; De'Von Achane reportedly out for season with torn ACL
item.description: Follow along with the latest NFL news coming out of Week 3.
item.content:encoded:
Another Sunday afternoon slate is in the books — and Week 3 was busy, ending with a bang as the Los Angeles Rams seemingly ended up on the end of a wrong DPI call that shifted the trajectory of their week. Unfortunately, it was also another Sunday that yielded several more injuries we'll have to monitor throughout the week.

Among the biggest to watch, particularly for fantasy managers, is a knee injury to Miami Dolphins running back De'Von Achane. He limped off after the first drive of the game and was eventually ruled out. ESPN's Adam Schefter reported Monday morning that Achane had suffered a torn ACL, with Miami now set to miss their star running back for the remainder of the 2026 season.

The Minnesota Vikings escaped with a win against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers despite losing All-Pro wide receiver Justin Jefferson to an ankle injury. Meanwhile, San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Mike Evans (rib) was also injured Sunday afternoon against the Arizona Cardinals before eventually being carted off after entering the week as questionable with a hip issue.

One team that can't blame their woes on an injury? The New England Patriots, who have the ultimate Super Bowl hangover, started the year 1-2 while quarterback Drake Maye struggles to gain his footing, currently tied to lead the league with four interceptions to pair with just a single passing touchdown.

item.title: J.J. McCarthy trade grades as Giants, Vikings swing QB deal
item.description: The Giants took bold action after Jaxson Dart's season-ending injury, landing J.J. McCarthy from the Vikings. But who won the deal?
item.content:encoded:
After the New York Giantslost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart to a season-ending knee injury, new coach John Harbaugh declared that the team was weighing "all options" at the position.

Less than a week later, that statement proved to be more than bluster.

On Monday, Sept. 28, the Giants agreed to a trade with the Minnesota Vikings, acquiring J.J. McCarthy in exchange for a 2027 fifth-round pick.

With the deal, New York added a starting-capable option for keeping its offense afloat if veteran fill-in Jameis Winston continues to struggle. Meanwhile, the Vikings officially close the door on a player who quickly fell out of the franchise's good graces following his turbulent lone campaign at the helm.

But which team fared better in the deal? Here's how each graded:

Giants' J.J. McCarthy trade grade: B-

On its face, obtaining the former No. 10 overall pick with two years left on his rookie contract for a mid-Day 3 selection seems like good business.

Of all the signal-callers the Giants could have acquired, McCarthy seems the least like a pure caretaker option. His pro track record, however, has been far from sterling. Not only have injuries severely inhibited his development, but his ball placement and decision-making were erratic enough to cost him his QB1 label after just one year at the helm.

Might he be the league's next salvage success story at his position?

In landing with a team facing a serious void behind center, this might have been the best possible short-term outcome for McCarthy. Harbaugh surely has both some intel and reason for belief in the former Michigan standout, who flourished under his brother, Jim Harbaugh. The Giants won't ask him to play the role of immediate savior, with Harbaugh having insisted last week that Winston would remain the team's starter even upon the addition of one or more additional passers.

Given Winston's struggles and rather wild accuracy, though, it hardly seems out of the question that McCarthy would at some point get his turn to show what he can do. Coordinator Matt Nagy might need to adjust the ask of a young quarterback who's far less likely to be a true catalyst than Dart was. Stringing together long drives and converting third downs repeatedly as Dart did in the opener might seem like a stretch for McCarthy, who's struggled with his consistency since entering the NFL. But Nagy might be able to harness McCarthy's ability to make plays on the move. Compensating for the team's lack of weaponry, however, might be difficult.

While New York could have afforded itself a higher floor with a more proven entity available on the market, such a move would have amounted to resignation of a lost season if Winston can't keep the offense at a workable level. McCarthy probably won't have a career renaissance in the span of a dozen or so games, but he at least provides some semblance of hope for an organization that has to evaluate its pieces and figure out where to go from here. The cost can't be fully written off – the Giants now only have five picks in next year's draft – but it's still rather modest.

Given where McCarthy is poised to begin his career with Big Blue, it's entirely too early to entertain any notion of him turning things around for himself or the offense. But beyond signing Jimmy Garoppolo, the Giants' alternative options weren't very inspiring, either.

Vikings' J.J. McCarthy trade grade: C+

In their public remarks on their struggling young signal-caller, both coach Kevin O'Connell and new general manager Nolan Teasley tried to remain upbeat when assessing McCarthy. The team's actual handling of him, however, proved much more revealing of their feelings.

Though Teasley earlier in September maintained McCarthy's "story is not written," the Vikings seemed to all but close the book on him with a demotion to the third string. That revealed what long seemed clear: O'Connell and Co. couldn't trust McCarthy.

The decision not to cut bait when setting the 53-man roster seemed less like a vote of confidence and more a matter of not wanting to come out completely empty-handed from an investment that went bust. A fifth-round pick isn't much of a return, but that likely speaks to the muted interest in McCarthy overall.

Given the injury troubles that have plagued both Kyler Murray and backup Carson Wentz – neither of whom is signed beyond this year, with the former unable to be franchise-tagged – Minnesota could see its already murky outlook at quarterback become even muddier. But if the organization was truly done with McCarthy, it was best to separate and no longer pay lip service to the notion of him ever playing a significant role again.

item.title: Did Cam Ward make a bad decision or a bad throw yesterday?
item.description: Either way, Ward would like to have that one back.
item.content:encoded:
Watching the Tennessee Titans’ final offensive play in real time yesterday, it looked to me like Cam Ward made a terrible decision to throw the ball. On the broadcast, it looked like there was a lot of room to run in front of him when he decided to throw the pass that was ultimately intercepted to end the game. After rewatching the play about 100 times, not running there was the smart play. There were two defenders between him and the end zone that would have stopped him.

The real issue was the throw. Here’s the final play:

Elic Ayomanor is running to the back left corner of the end zone. As old friend SuperHorn mentions, if Ward throws it to that corner, Jevon Holland has no chance to pick it off, and Ayomanor would have had a chance to catch it for a touchdown. The real problem is the accuracy of the throw. Watch it again. There is no shot that ball Ward threw was getting completed, even if he is able to throw it over Holland.

With that being said, I also don’t think Ward was being reckless with the ball here. As I mentioned above, a throw to the corner is either a touchdown or an incomplete pass. That means they win the game or live to play another down – which would have been 2nd and goal from the 7.

Ward has done more wrong than right this year. The thing that is really starting to scare me is his overall inconsistency. There have still been flashes of a solid quarterback in there, but he can’t put that together consistently from play to play, much less from game to game. The only way he is going to be a franchise quarterback is to play consistently. Through 20 NFL games, he has not shown the ability to do that.

item.title: The Vikings swung and missed in effort to find a franchise quarterback
item.description: After the 2023 season, the Vikings decided to abandon the veteran quarterback rollercoaster for a potential franchise quarterback.
item.content:encoded:
After the 2023 season, the Vikings decided to abandon the veteran quarterback rollercoaster for a potential franchise quarterback.

The ride ended up being bumper cars without the bumpers.

Minnesota had earned the 11th overall pick in the 2024 draft. Four quarterbacks had been drafted in the first eight picks. As the clock ticked toward their pick at No. 11, the Vikings feared being leapfrogged by the Broncos at No. 12.

And so the Vikings gave up a fourth-round pick and a fifth-round pick to move up from No. 11 to No. 10. (They also received a seventh-rounder from the Jets as part of the deal.) They used the pick not to take Oregon quarterback Bo Nix, but to select Michigan quarterback J.J. McCarthy.

His rookie season was lost to a meniscus injury during the preseason opener. And while the 2024 season went well with free-agent Sam Darnold stepping in, the Vikings opted to go all-in with McCarthy for 2025, allowing both Darnold and Daniel Jones to leave via free agency.

McCarthy won his debut game on a Monday night in Chicago. A Week 2 loss in Atlanta resulted in an ankle injury that caused McCarthy to miss the next five games. He returned in Week 9 with an upset of the Lions in Detroit. Three straight losses followed, and a concussion in Green Bay caused McCarthy to miss what was a 26-0 low point in Seattle with undrafted rookie Max Brosmer at the helm.

But then McCarthy returned. He won three in a row, missed the Christmas Day win over the Lions (Brosmer got a little redemption, but not much, in the defense-driven performance), and won the regular-season finale against the Packers. While the Vikings' postseason hopes were dashed after the shutout loss to the Seahawks, the Vikings finished strong under McCarthy.

Still, the two-year body of work wasn't enough to keep the Vikings from pouncing on the opportunity to add Kyler Murray in free agency, on a bargain-basement deal (thanks to the Cardinals owing him more than $35 million in 2026). The competition between Murray and McCarthy lingered into training camp, with Murray getting the job in the days before the preseason opener.

At that point, it seemed that a fresh start for McCarthy would be beneficial for both sides. The vibes were clearly off, even though the team and the player did their best to conceal any dysfunction. The fact that McCarthy slipped behind Carson Wentz on the depth chart underscored the reality that it was just a matter of time before McCarthy would be gone.

Opportunity knocked after the Giants lost Jaxson Dart to a knee injury. Still, the Vikings got merely a fifth-round pick for McCarthy — after giving up the 11th pick in 2024, a fourth-round pick, and a fifth-round pick to get him (with the seventh-round pick in return).

It's always prudent for a team that has made a mistake to admit it and move on. Doubling down helps no one. Still, there's a price to be paid for acknowledging to such a major blunder.

And while no one knows what was happening behind the scenes, the early-season performances from Murray and Wentz suggested that maybe, at some point in 2026, the Vikings would have needed McCarthy to play. His absence puts more pressure on the team to make it work with Murray and/or Wentz (and, if necessary, with Brosmer).

The Vikings also need to quietly hope that McCarthy doesn't become a competent contributor for the Giants. If he does, the Vikings would join the list of franchises that used a high pick on a rookie quarterback, failed to develop him, and folded the tents prematurely.

item.title: Giants to waive QB Jake Haener, intend to re-sign him to practice squad
item.description: With the Giants trading for J.J.
item.content:encoded:
With the Giants trading for J.J. McCarthy, the club will make another roster move to keep just two quarterbacks on their 53-man roster.

Per Mike Garafolo of NFL Network, New York will waive Jake Haener but intend to re-sign him to the team's practice squad.

Haener was promoted to the active roster on Saturday after Jaxson Dart suffered a long-term knee injury last Monday night.

Haener, 27, joined the Giants in August after spending some time with the Chiefs during the offseason program.

A fourth-round pick in 2023, Haener has appeared in eight career games with one start. All of his appearances came in 2024 with the Saints.

item.title: Game Recap: Saints host Raiders in home opener
item.description: Catch up on all of Sunday’s action from New Orleans.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints at last played their home opener when they hosted the Las Vegas Raiders in the late window on Sunday afternoon. Here’s a look back at all that went down in the Caesars Superdome.

First Quarter

The hosts received the opening kickoff but went three-and-out.

The Raiders, meanwhile, found instant momentum as Kirk Cousins completed his first four throws for 53 yards, including three receptions by tight end Brock Bowers who was suiting up for the first time this season.

But after an offensive holding and a sack by Chase Young, the defense was able to hold Vegas to a field goal attempt. Matt Gay converted from 41 yards.

The Saints faced another quick three-and-out as they began their ensuing series, but a huge 3rd down scramble from Tyler Shough for 36 yards kicked the offense into life.

Travis Etienne Jr had some work on the ground, and Shough found Devaughn Vele and Chris Olave for double-digit gains as the Saints entered the red zone.

CJ Donaldson would then run for 5 yards to set up a 2-yard touchdown throw from Shough to Juwan Johnson.

Daniel Carlson’s extra point was blocked by his former team, so the score remained 6-3.

Second Quarter

The Raiders began their next drive at the 40 after the kickoff fell short of the landing zone. They drove past midfield with a run from Mike Washington, before Cousins found Michael Mayer for 18 yards.

An offside penalty helped the defensive effort as the Saints were able to force another field goal attempt, which Gay converted from 37 yards to tie the game at 6-6.

New Orleans then went three-and-out, and punted to the visitors who began the ensuing possession at midfield.

The Raiders took full advantage, with Cousins continuing to find Mayer and Bowers as they entered the red zone.

The Saints thought they’d done enough to keep Vegas out of the end zone again, but a roughing the passer penalty against Danny Stutsman for what looked like a perfect hit on the quarterback gave the Raiders 1st-and-goal.

Cousins found Mayer for the 3-yard score, and the visitors took a 13-6 lead.

Etienne had a few short gains on the ground to begin the Saints’ next possession, before Shough found Olave twice in a row for a total of 29 yards. He then found his tight ends Noah Fant and Johnson, before another short run from Etienne put the ball at the 3-yard line.

Shough found Fant in the end zone for the score, and Carlson’s extra point levelled the game at 13-13.

Cousins ran a successful two-minute drill before the half, helped by another pair of big gains through Bowers. A 25-yard field goal from Gay gave Vegas a 16-13 lead as time expired.

Third Quarter

The Raiders went three-and-out to begin the second half.

Shough continued to have success moving the football as he returned to the field, with passes to Vele and Etienne alongside runs from Alvin Kamara moving the black and gold past midfield.

Shough continued to sling it, connecting with Johnson, Vele, and Olave to move the hosts to the 1-yard line.

It was Johnson again who caught another touchdown pass, continuing the game of the tight-ends.

Trailing 20-16, the Raiders return-man Dylan Laube then fumbled the kickoff return. The Saints recovered, and took instant advantage.

Etienne broke out a 16-yard run before Shough threw to Fant for a 16-yard touchdown pass, and just like that the hosts were up 27-16.

But the Raiders did well to respond, as Bowers continued his dominant display with a 20-yard catch to move the drive past midfield. Before long, Washington ran in a 36-yard touchdown to cut into the lead.

After an unsuccessful 2-point conversion attempt, the score remained 27-22.

The team exchanged quick punts after that, before an 11-yard pass from Shough to Olave on 3rd down extended the ensuing series for the black and gold and put them into Vegas territory.

Fourth Quarter

Shough converted another 3rd down to Olave a few plays later.

But with the Saints on the edge of field goal range, Shough was sacked and stripped by Malcolm Koonce as he intended to throw, in the same fashion that Chase Young got to Jared Goff in Week 1. The fumble was recovered by the defense, but this time, the ruling on the field stood and Vegas would take over.

Cousins found Ashton Jeanty for 22 yards to begin the drive, before connecting with Tre Tucker for 15 yards a few plays later.

Cody White would catch the short touchdown to restore the lead for the visitors. After another failed 2-point conversion, they led just 28-27.

But the Saints’ woes would then continue as Shough’s pass for Bryce Lance was picked off by Hezekiah Masses. Masses then fumbled himself, but the Raiders fell on it again and had 1st-and-goal from the 4-yard line.

The Saints stopped Jeanty twice before on 3rd down Cousins connected with Bowers in the end zone, and the Raiders went up 35-27.

Still just a one-score game, the Saints did promptly enter the red zone helped by runs from Kamara and a 22-yard throw to Johnson.

But Shough fumbled as he was sacked again, with Maxx Crosby forcing the ball out.

The defense forced the Raiders into a quick punt to keep hopes alive. But in the two-minute drill, Johnson fumbled after a catch near midfield as turnovers continued to mount for the black and gold.

The Raiders jumped on it, and knelt out the clock from there to secure a 35-27 win.

The Saints’ focus now turns to Monday Night Football when they host the Atlanta Falcons in a week’s time.

item.title: Giants acquire J.J. McCarthy from Vikings for 2027 fifth-round pick
item.description: New York adds depth after Jaxson Dart was ruled out for the season due to a knee injury.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants are acquiring quarterback J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings in exchange for a 2027 fifth-round pick.

McCarthy had been serving as the third-string quarterback in Minnesota behind Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz. New York adds depth at quarterback after starter Jaxson Dart was ruled out for the remainder of the regular season due to a torn MCL and meniscus.

New York started veteran Jameis Winston and called up Jake Haener to serve as his backup in the Week 3 win over the Titans. Even though the Giants picked up their second win of the season, Winston struggled, and New York's 12 points were from four field goals.

With the acquisition, the Giants have waived Haener and intend to bring him back on the practice squad. It seems that the intention is for McCarthy to, at worst, back up Winston in Week 4 against the Arizona Cardinals.

This move gets McCarthy a fresh start as the 23-year-old is still in just his third year in the league. The former Michigan Wolverine played for Jim Harbaugh in college and will now play for his brother, John Harbaugh, with the Giants.

McCarthy missed his entire rookie season due to a torn MCL that he suffered in the 2024 NFL preseason. Last year, made his regular-season debut, going 6-4 over his 10 starts. The QB finished with 1,632 passing yards, 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions. Injuries also continued to plague McCarthy in his second season, missing five games with a high-ankle sprain and another game down the stretch with a concussion.

Winston took over for Dart during the team's 28-6 loss to the Rams. He struggled mightily, completing only 11-of-27 passes for 111 yards. The 32-year-old Winston was sacked twice and threw a second-quarter interception while in the red zone.

A backup for the last several years, Winston was once the top pick in the draft, back in 2015. That marked the beginning of his five-season run as the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' QB1. Winston, a Heisman Trophy and national championship winner at Florida State, earned Pro Bowl honors as a rookie and led the NFL with 5,109 passing yards in 2019. That season, though, he infamously tossed 30 interceptions to go along with his 33 touchdown strikes.

On-field decision-making has held back Winston throughout his pro career. The Winston experience is a roller coaster, for better or worse. He can chuck the ball around the yard, as evidenced by his 25,021 career passing yards — a total he previously added to amid stints with the New Orleans Saints (2020-23) and Cleveland Browns (2024) before he joined the Giants ahead of last season — but he's notoriously turnover-prone.

That said, he's known for his infectious personality, unrelenting positivity as a leader and for his ability to spark an offense. Earlier this month, the Giants inked Winston to a two-year extension through 2028 that's reportedly worth $13 million. Harbaugh has gone to bat for the veteran this week.

"He can throw it," Harbaugh said last Wednesday of Winston. "He's a big, strong passing quarterback. He can throw the ball. Everybody that follows football has certainly seen Jameis play, and his strengths are evident.

Winston finished the Week 3 win going 14 of 22 passing for 118 yards with no touchdowns or interceptions. He scrambled twice for 14 yards and was sacked three times.

New York has four more games until its Week 8 bye week. That could be when, depending on how Winston plays over the next month, the Giants could make a move to get McCarthy under center.

item.title: Giants made the one QB trade that offered hope, even if it doesn't guarantee anything
item.description: Trading for McCarthy makes some short- and long-term success, even if it's still not guaranteed to work.
item.content:encoded:
When news broke that Jaxson Dart was done for the season and that the New York Giants were shopping for quarterback help, it was hard not to think: Good luck.

Quarterbacks don't grow on trees. Smart teams don't let good ones out of the building often, at least not for cheap.

But there was one available option to the Giants, trading for J.J. McCarthy, that at least offered a glimmer of hope. Will it work? That remains a stretch, based on how McCarthy has played to this point.

Yet it at least has a chance to work, which is likely better than you can say about the other options the Giants had at their disposal. Most of them were short-term rentals. Most of them were older and more experienced, but there was a reason they were either unemployed or available by trade.

McCarthy's circumstances are unique. He's a recent (high) first-round pick who clearly fell out of favor with the Minnesota Vikings, who appeared quite willing to move on from him. The cost (a 2027 fifth-rounder) was pretty indicative of that, selling for quarters on the dollar after a little more than two years of him being in the building.

Somehow, McCarthy fell from competing for the Vikings' starting job in mid-August to being their QB3 by early September. It was telling that Carson Wentz, not McCarthy, was Kyler Murray's backup when he was knocked out of Minnesota's Week 1 game. McCarthy's problems weren't all football-related, either. He'd clearly lost the trust of the Vikings' coaching staff, one that has cobbled together functional offenses with less-credentialed QBs before.

That's a reminder of where McCarthy was prior to the trade: the third QB option on a team that ranks dead last in the NFL in total yards, pass yards and first downs. It should also serve as a warning for any Giants fans counting on this saving their season.

Granted, the bar is pretty low for the post-Dart Giants. Jameis Winston struggled badly against the Rams after Dart was injured and was passable at best on Sunday in a close-shave win over the Titans at home. Four field goals and 238 yards of offense might work vs. Tennessee, but it's probably not going to cut it much going forward, with the toughest part of the Giants' schedule upcoming.

Why McCarthy was the one trade option that made some sense

There were plenty of dots to connect between McCarthy and the Giants, so this is far from a shocking trade. He played for Jim Harbaugh at Michigan and now gets brother John; this is not the first time they've swapped players, and even coaches. The Giants also did ample background work on McCarthy prior to the 2024 NFL Draft and appeared to like him then.

They clearly like something about McCarthy now, even if his situation has changed dramatically. One, he was cheap. Two, he's a young QB at age 23 — four months older than Dart — who's only had 10 starts to show himself. The Giants said they wanted to add an "experienced" quarterback, so it remains to be seen if this is the experience level they were actually seeking, but this trade also has some potential long-term benefits, too.

Yes, McCarthy is being brought in to help this season. There was a real question how long they could stuck with Winston, and they were one hit away from playing Jake Haener. So you can bet the Giants will throw the kitchen sink at McCarthy and see how he responds. The Giants have games against the Cardinals, Commanders and Texans prior to the Week 8 bye. The next month will tell us a lot about how quickly the Giants plan to bring McCarthy into the fold.

But the trade also offers a bit of long-term insurance. Dart will have missed 17 of 34 games with injury by season's end. The concussions were a major Year 1 storyline, and the knee has been the headline for Year 2. Even with aggressive rehab, he still could be limited early next offseason, and the Giants likely knew they need better contingency plans.

Can McCarthy provide that? Maybe. The results to this point are what they are. The Giants will take a little ugly if McCarthy can deliver some victories, even if they look as sluggish as the one Winston helped deliver Sunday. But they clearly want to see improvement on what he did with the Vikings, and that means getting better with Giants offensive personnel that is arguably no more or less impressive than what Minnesota has.

If McCarthy plays well enough, he could be in the Giants' 2027 mix. Dart remains the franchise QB until proven otherwise, and McCarthy's arrival could complicate matters down the road. Some trades have costs that go beyond draft-pick compensation and salary, and this is one of them. Will Dart feel threatened by McCarthy's arrival. It'll be interesting to hear what the Giants say about this and whether they consulted Dart before making the trade.

The Giants now will inherit a looming decision next summer on McCarthy's fifth-year option, which also would be tough to green light even if McCarthy plays well. For now, they can afford McCarthy's first-round salary this year and next, even if, interestingly enough, he'll make a shade more money than Dart will.

Those are more trivial details for now, though. The bottom line is that the Giants are gambling on McCarthy's talent and intangibles, even if there might be a lot to clean up — those late eyes and forced balls we've seen too much of speak for themselves. Coaching him up for starter-level duty will require some serious fast tracking from this staff.

There were more immediately ready options available that didn't require picks to be traded — hired-gun free-agent quarterbacks who have previously joined other teams in a pinch and readied themselves for quick action. No one would have blamed the Giants if they went out and signed Jimmy Garoppolo or Brandon Allen or a similar-ilk QB.

Trading for McCarthy was a clear break from that strategy. It appears the Giants are as worried about tomorrow as they are about today. The problem? This trade doesn't guarantee that either concern will be fully addressed. That is the risk, even for such a relatively low-cost trade.

item.title: Panthers could be down 2 key defensive backs vs. Lions
item.description: The Carolina Panthers could be missing both starting cornerbacks in their Sunday night game against the Detroit Lions.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions are entering Week 4 as three-point favorites over the Carolina Panthers in their Sunday night showdown, but some injury news from Monday could see that line shift (note: it’s already jumped to 3.5). According to NFL reporter Tom Pelissero, the Panthers’ No. 1 cornerback Jaycee Horn is out indefinitely after suffering a quad injury on Sunday against the Browns.

Horn is coming off back-to-back Pro Bowl seasons with the Panthers, and he signed a four-year, $100 million extension last offseason. He was off to another decent start to the season, allowing just five catches on 10 targets for 63 yard and two pass breakups, according to PFF.

To make matters worse for the Panthers, in Sunday’s loss to the Browns, they also lost their other starting outside cornerback Mike Jackson to a groin injury. There has yet to be an update on his status, but he suffered the injury in the first half and did not return to the game. Jackson is an eight-year vet who actually spent some brief time with the Lions in 2019, but has really turned things around lately. In 2025, Jackson produced an NFL-high 19 passes defended and also logged four interception.

Left in the Panthers’ cornerback room is fourth-round rookie Will Lee III, Akayleb Evans, and nickel corner Chau Smith-Wade. Carolina also has three practice squad cornerbacks: undrafted rookie DeVonta Smith, and two undrafted players from the 2025 class: Zion Childress and Corey Thornton. Of the three, only Thornton has any real experience at the NFL level, playing in 12 games and 127 defensive snaps last season.

This will be something to monitor as the week goes on, but I would expect the Panthers to add to that room as they prepare for a dynamic Detroit Lions passing attack that currently ranks eighth in passing yards (247.7 per game), third in passer rating (116.1), and tied for second in passing touchdowns (eight).

item.title: Jaxon Smith-Njigba off to historic start in 2026
item.description: The superstar wideout joined elite company on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Though the Seattle Seahawks were upset by the Washington Commanders on Sunday, one constant remained even as an upset occurred.

Reigning Offensive Player of the Year Jaxon Smith-Njigba showed up in a major way for the Seahawks, posting 10 catches for 128 yards and two touchdowns in a losing effort. For Smith-Njigba, it was more of the same — and kept him on a historic path to begin the 2026 season.

According to Seahawks PR, Smith-Njigba became the fourth player in the Super Bowl era with six touchdowns across the first three games of a season, after Calvin Johnson (2011), Marvin Harrison (1999), and Daryl Turner (1985). Narrowing that scope to include thresholds of 25+ catches and 400+ yards, Smith-Njigba is the second player after just Harrison in ’99 to hit those marks.

Smith Njigba’s consistency has him in incredible company, too. According to ESPN Insights, on Sunday he joined Jerry Rice as the only players in history to post 120 yards and a touchdown in each of his team’s first three games. With another 100-yard, touchdown day next Sunday, he will join Randy Moss as the only players to start the season with four straight games with 100 yards and a touchdown.

After dropping a game it shouldn’t have on Sunday, Seattle is a good bet to bounce back back at home against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 4. Just as likely is for Smith-Njigba to play a major part, and continue to make history for the Seahawks.

item.title: J.J. McCarthy trade: Giants acquire quarterback from Minnesota Vikings
item.description: The Giants make a bold move for young quarterback.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants are acquiring quarterback J.J. McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings, per a report from NFL insider Ian Rapoport.

Per Jordan Schultz, the Giants are sending a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Vikings for McCarthy. The Vikings have confirmed the trade.

The Giants, of course, lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season with a knee injury during their Week 2 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. Jameis Winston’s play since has been uninspiring, and the only other quarterback on the roster was journeyman Jake Haener.

The Giants had an opportunity to draft the 23-year-old McCarthy out of Michigan with the sixth overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft. They passed on McCarthy, as well as Bo Nix and Michael Penix, to select wide receiver Malik Nabers. The Vikings took McCarthy No. 10 overall.

That, of course, worked out well for the Giants. Nabers had a sensational rookie season, and the Giants were able to move up in the 2025 NFL Draft to select Dart as their quarterback of the future.

Things did not go well for McCarthy in Minnesota.

McCarthy missed all of his rookie season with a torn meniscus in his right knee. He started 10 games for the Vikings last season, compiling a 6-4 record. He completed 140 of 243 passes (jusy 57.6%) for 1,623 yards with 11 touchdowns, 12 interceptions and a 72.6 passer rating.

This offseason, the Vikings signed veteran Kyler Murray as a free agent. McCarthy not only lost a competition with Murray for the starting job, but ended up as the No. 3 quarterback in Minnesota behind Murray and Carson Wentz.

Now, he will join the Giants.

In his recently-launched Substack, ‘The Sweep’, NFL insider Tom Pelissero said this about why the Giants made the deal:

The Giants extensively scouted McCarthy (and the rest of the 2024 quarterback class) before deciding to wait and taking Dart in 2025. McCarthy’s athletic ability and play style is a fit for the offense that OC Matt Nagy and company built for Dart, and he should be capable of running many of the QB movement concepts that figure to be dormant as long as Winston, a pocket passer, is in the lineup. At age 23, McCarthy is less than four months older than Dart. He’s 6-4 as an NFL starter. He’s cost-controlled for 2027. And in the event McCarthy takes over and flourishes down the stretch this season, the Giants have the right to exercise his fifth-year option for 2028.

Valentine’s View

While I figured the Giants were going to be aggressive in the quarterback market after McCarthy’s injury, this is not a move I expected them to make.

The Giants spent a massive amount of time with McCarthy prior to the 2024 draft, concluding in the end that he was not the right quarterback for them.

Maybe the Dart injury, and what they saw on the market made them view McCarthy differently. Maybe John Harbaugh had a different impression of McCarthy than Joe Schoen and the Giants’ scouts when the Ravens studied him in 2024. Maybe Harbaugh’s brother, Jim, gave his brother a glowing recommendation of McCarthy.

Jay Glazer is reporting that John Harbaugh did speak to his brother about McCarthy before the Giants made the deal.

Maybe the idea of adding another 23-year-old quarterback with NFL experience and upside was too good for the Giants to pass up. Both as a hedge against Winston’s ups and downs, and perhaps as a long-term option if Dart doesn’t become what the Giants believe he will.

I have mixed feelings about the trade. If McCarthy couldn’t handle Minnesota or succeed with quarterback guru Kevin O’Connell as his coach, what makes the Giants believe he can succeed in New York? Does this open them to questions about whether they full believe in Dart’s future?

I can’t blame them for taking a big swing and getting the best quarterback they could get. And, I certainly think this is a better swing than Justin Fields or Gardner Minshew. It just comes with a lot of questions.

Vote in the poll and let us know what you think of the move, Giants fans.

I watched yesterday’s game where the Miami Dolphins fell to the KC Chiefs 10-10 and the NFL referees 14-0. The combined score was KC/NFL Refs 24 – Miami/out of favors 10.  I can’t even talk about the Dolphins performance until I unpack the completed slanted officiating.

Unless the “anointed team” completely no shows, the refs in every sport will put their hoofs on the scales of justice to benefit whatever team is anointed. I remember the Heat beating the Chicago Bulls in Jordan’s heyday at the old Miami Arena. I was in attendance. Steffi Graf, Jack Nickalus, Cal Ripken, Jr. and I think Ferdie Pacheco were also there to watch the GOAT.  However, Rex Champman hit like 7 or 8 3-pointers and the Heat beat down the Bulls. If the game would’ve been closer, the refs would have carried the Bulls over the finish line as they usually did for MJ.

We saw this in full effect today. The NFL officiating is the biggest embarrassment in the history of the American experience. There is no attempt to improve it. It really makes you think that the NFL decides who will win each game before the season begins in some type of Star Chamber (check out this Michael Douglas movie if you can). In the olden days in England, powerful folks would meet outside at night under the stars to decide the guilt or innocence of some individual and then they would carry out the sentence(hence the term Star Chamber). It makes you think the powers that be have money on the game. I could literally write a hundred pages on how many garbage calls have went against the Dolphins over the last 40 years. I know other teams get screwed too but our pendulum is stuck to the bad. Many of these calls are simply inexplicable. And if you complain, the NFL punishes you. I still do not understand how the NFL gets aways with this, KNOWING they have an anti-trust exemption from the U.S. government. In what other American endeavor outside of sports can a member of that organization NOT criticize a corporation publicly? If I worked at Acme and criticized them, yes they would fire me and rightfully so and I can go public if I have evidence of their wrong doing However, again Acme does not have an anti-trust exemption or at least that is what the Coyote told me 😊. There is NOTHING less American than the NFL stifling free speech.

The NFL practices in gross negligence and then has the buffoonish broadcasters and their “so called officiating expert” Gene Steratore come out and bless every single call. For those of you who don’t know, Steratore was the absolute buffoon moron who screwed the Dolphins against the Steelers in Miami (2010, I think) where the Steelers fumbled the ball in the end zone, THE FINS RECOVERED THE DAMN BALL, and this complete moron said there wasn’t a clear recovery and gave the ball back to the Steelers. It turns out this guy grew up in Pittsburgh and was allowed to ref an NFL with the Steelers. How in the name of God can this happen? So, this is the buffoon who was asked about the sissy roughing the passer call against Chop Robinson? This was a total garbage call because what was Chop supposed to do, sack Mahomes and use his “Homelander” super powers to fly away at the last nano-second? Momentum and gravity made Chop land on Mahomes, not intent. But Mahomes is the anointed one by the NFL, just like Brady was. It you launch an “air biscuit” against Brady or Mahomes it is an automatic 15-yard penalty. They cannot be touched. Period. So Steratore weighed in on that one but where was Steratore when Malik’s helmet was pulled off? Nowhere to be found. Where was Steratore when the player pulled Achane’s facemask on the play where he was hurt? Nowhere to be found. The NFL officiating cannot be criticized and it NEVER makes a mistake. In the legal world, attorneys must avoid EVEN the appearance of impropriety. Not the NFL.

In my many travels to London, I noticed many stores (usually the elite ones like Harrod’s) have these shields up on the top corner of the store entrances. I asked what those were and I was told there was an official process to apply for the shield. These shields let the general public know that this business is preferred by the royal family; I just read that they had to be updated for the transition to King Charles. So I want to figure out how the Dolphins can earn the NFL preferred shield? Do we need to run ads with Malik’s and Devon’s shirts off? item.title: We’re witnessing a different breed of Raiders as team drops Saints 35-27
item.description: Klint Kubiak’s football team rises to occasion instead of wilting as complementary football overshadows mistakes in win
item.content:encoded:
How easy would it have been for the Silver & Black to wilt after the opposition not only scored a touchdown to take the lead, but recovered the fumble on the ensuing kick off, and two plays later, made another end zone visit.

But Klint Kubiak, his coaching staff, and players apparently don’t like to do things “easy”.

For the third straight game on the young 2026 season, Kubiak’s Las Vegas Raiders stared down adversity in the face, smirked, got the job done. This time, it was on the road against the New Orleans Saints, and instead of succumbing to quick-sand situations the Raiders were well-accustomed to do in year’s past, Las Vegas answered the ball, rose to the occasion, and earned an impressive 35-27 victory.

Once more we saw complementary Raiders football where the defense picked up the offense and vice versa, despite special teams gaffes. Instead of collapsing under the immense pressure — on the road against a quailty New Orleans squad, Las Vegas persevered and won.

The performances and results harken on the old adage: Once is an accident, twice is a coincidence, three times is a pattern. The first time the Raiders showcased resolve to win in the season opener against the Miami Dolphins was eyebrow raising. The second time they did it by beating the Los Angeles Chargers piqued interest. Doing it for the third time at New Orleans certainly firmly establishes a pattern.

And it harkens on this: We’re witnessing a different breed of Silver & Black with Kubiak at the helm.

After trading touchdowns in the second quarter to knot the score at 13, Las Vegas moved the ball into the red zone during a two-minute drill and hit a field goal to take a 16-13 lead into halftime. The potential double-dip was thwarted, however, as the Raiders did receive the second-half kick off only to go three-and-out.

And this began the downward spiral for the Silver & Black.

Kellen Moore’s Saints offense went on an impressive 12-play, 87-yard touchdown drive that chewed 6:50 off the clock. And with 20-16 lead in hand, New Orleans scooped up in inexplicable fumble by Las Vegas running back and kick return man Dylan Laube. Like noted above, two plays and 32 yards later, Saints quarterback Tyler Shough found tight end Noah Fant for a 16-yard touchdown, 27-16 New Orleans.

Instead of wallowing in the series of unfortunate events, however, Kubiak’s offense ran five plays culminating in rookie running back Mike Washington Jr. finding daylight and immolating New Orleans defense on a 36-yard touchdown run. Trailing just 27-22 after the two teams traded punts to close the third quarter, the Saints went on a spiral of their own.

As our Matt Holder noted shortly after the game, all four of the Saints’ possessions in the fourth quarter ended in turnovers. That great equalizer gave the Raiders ample runway for two final stanza touchdowns — a four-yard touchdown strike from quarterback Kirk Cousins to wide receiver Cody White and four-yard dime from Cousins to tight end Brock Bowers, 35-27 Las Vegas.

Let’s hit the quick slants as fast as Rob Leonard’s Raiders defense took the ball away from the Saints:

—Cousins went 22 of 33 for 248 yards with three touchdowns, no interceptions, while getting sacked three times against the Saints. The veteran quarterback has thrown three touchdown passes in the first trio of games validating Kubiak’s decision to roll with the 38-year-old signal caller over No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza.

—“Brock-tober Fest” arrived early as Bowers’ had an outstanding season debut with 10 catches for 116 yards and one touchdown. The tight end lined up all over the formation from traditional in-line and split tight end and even in the slot and perimeter that’s normally reserved for a wide receiver.

—Raiders starting running back Ashton Jeanty carried the rock 19 times for 56 yards and a paltry 2.9 yards per carry average. One has to wonder if his ankle is 100 percent but Washington provided juice of his own with five carries for 54 yards including the scintillating touchdown.

—Linebacker Nakobe Dean is proving the Raiders wise for giving him a big-money deal in free agency as the veteran paced the team with 12 total tackles, a stop for loss, and a forced fumble to slam the door on the Saints collective faces. This after he forced a key fumble to help Las Vegas win last week.

—Leonard’s defense forced four turnovers from the Saints. A trio were forced fumbles — two on sacks; one from defensive end Malcolm Koonce and the other from strong safety Jeremy Chinn — and the other an interception by rookie cornerback Hezekiah Masses (his third pick on the young season).

—Getting rookie safety Treydan Stukes back in the Raiders secondary can’t happen soon enough. Inactive due to a concussion sustained in Week 2, veteran Isaiah Pola-Mao got the start and the Saints picked on him frequently as he was charted giving up three of Shough’s four touchdown passes.

Quotes of Note

“When I hit him, I saw the ball come up. I thought the ball was going forward so I just assumed it was a strip sack. It was very rewarding. We knew whole time (in) the second half, we knew the defense was going to have to show up.”

—Las Vegas Raiders defensive end Malcolm Koonce on his forced fumble

“We knew we had to rally back, we had to start back playing our type of football. And that’s our style of play, taking the ball away. We got a goal every week, ‘How many takeaways are we going to get?’ We had none in the first half, so we had to come back in the second half strong.”

—Las Vegas Raiders middle linebacker Nakobe Dean on defense’s mentality

Up Next

It’s a battle of AFC West unbeatens next Sunday when the Raiders (3-0) host the unbeaten Kansas City Chiefs (3-0) who picked up their first road win of the season with a 24-10 victory over the Miami Dolphins this past Sunday. Powered by Patrick Mahomes efficient afternoon and running back Kenneth Walker III’s two-touchdown outing (one rushing, another receiving) the Chiefs sit atop the division alongside the Raiders. It’s an AFC West that features Kansas City and Las Vegas on top, the Denver Broncos at 2-1 and the Los Angeles Chargers at 0-3.

item.title: Game balls for the Broncos comeback win over the LA Rams
item.description: The Denver Broncos slept through the first half and went Thanos mode in the second to beat the Los Angles Rams in Week 3. Here are our game balls.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos replicated the kind of magic it had last year in that 33-point fourth quarter nuke it dropped on the New York Giants. Except this time, they executed a comeback against a true Super Bowl contender in the Los Angeles Rams, which makes the comeback even more impressive than that one last year.

The game was a tale of two halves — seems like that is a typical statement with these Broncos — with the Rams completely dominating and smothering Denver on both sides of the ball for a 16-0 halftime lead. The caveat being that the Broncos’ defense made all of the red zone stops it needed to keep hope alive heading into the third quarter.

The third quarter had plenty of lucky breaks for the Broncos, including a fumble that turned into a bigger gain. They scored touchdowns and two-point conversions in back-to-back drives to tie the game and swing all of the momentum their way and they would close out the win with more big plays in the fourth quarter. It was a heckuva comeback win and the drama lasted to the final play.

Here’s who we’re giving our game balls to:

Talanoa Hufanga

Talanoa Hufanga gets my game ball this week. He made a game-changing pick-six right after the Broncos had lost momentum. He sealed the game on the last play with another interception. He had a chance at another interception earlier in the game that he dropped, but made plays when it mattered. He also had an absolutely beautifully timed safety blitz to blow up Stafford and force a field goal on a 3rd and long. Safeties don’t get games much better than what we saw from Hufanga this week. Fa’afetai tele, Talanoa! – Sadaraine

Bo Nix

My game ball goes to Bo Nix, after a forgettable first half in which he had two interception worthy throws that should have been picked, Bo came out and put on a show in the second half. Nix was 6/12 for 53 yards in the first half. The Broncos had four drives, two of which were three and out. The one drive with any potency ended with a doinked 43 yard FG. While Bo was only 11/22 for 133 yards in the second half, he made the throws when he needed to. Like this throw on the second 2-pt conversion:

Bo also accounted for all three of the Bronco TDs on the game throwing for two and running for one. The Bronco second half drives after the 3-and-out to start the half: TD, TD, INT, punt, TD. – Joe Mahoney

Pat Bryant

My game ball goes to Pat Bryant. He had a touchdown catch, a two-point conversion, and a 39-yard catch and run that put the Broncos in scoring position late in the fourth quarter. Every time he was targeted, he came down with the ball. Bryant was also on point recovering a J.K. Dobbins fumble in the game to advance it and keep the Rams from making it a turnover. Hopefully his performance tonight is the sign bigger things are still in store for the talented second-year wide receiver. – Chris Hart

Brandon Jones

Talanoa Hufanga stole the show on the big play front, but it was Brandon Jones mopping up the dirty work on the field. He finished with 12 total tackles, a tackle for a loss, a pass defensed, and a quarterback hit. Both safeties played an outstanding game after the first half struggles and in the red zone they dominated. I was tempted to give my game ball to the officiating crew for that bogus DPI call, but we’ve been screwed by plenty a questionable call so I’ll just call that one a small payout for all the other bad calls that went against Denver. – Tim Lynch

Davis Webb

After that dismal first half against LA, Broncos Country was ready for Sean Payton to take the play calling back from Webb. No rhythm. No flow. The offense looked like it had never played before. But as bad as Denver’s offense was in the first half, it was even better in the second. And Webb is a big reason why. The young play caller dialed up some fantastic plays and Nix and the Broncos executed masterfully. There’s always going to be growing pains and a learning curve with a young playcaller, but this should give Webb, the team, and the fanbase the confidence he’s got this. – Ian St. Clair

Zach Allen

Zach Allen has been a monster through 3 weeks. He notched his 3rd sack of the season against the Rams, but that and his 2 tackles fall well short of telling the full tale of Allen’s impact on the game. The Broncos’ disruptive defensive end was a headache for LA all evening, clogging up the defensive center and keeping Matt Stafford uncomfortable. – Taylor Kothe

Who gets your game ball for the Broncos-Rams game? Share in the comments section below.

item.title: Eagles at Bears: 3 Props to Play
item.description: The Chicago Bears face the Philadelphia Eagles on MNF. Here are 3 props to play.
item.content:encoded:
Well, the prop master (self-titled, of course) took a brutal beating last week. After our typical 2-1 outcome in week 1, we followed that up with a 0-3 burger in week 2. That drops our season record to 2-4 and puts us below .500 for the first time in over two seasons.

But we look to have a better week in week three. The Bears play tonight on Monday Night Football as they welcome the Philadelphia Eagles. Here are three props we like this week. Odds courtesy of FanDuel.

Kyle Monangai OVER 38.5 Rushing Yards -113

The Chicago Bears are going to have Case Keenum run the offense this week, and I think the one thing we know is that Ben Johnson is going to focus on getting the run game going and try to take some of the pressure off Keenum. The Eagles have given up some yards on the ground this year, and Monangai diced them up last year. I don’t think Monangai runs for 130 again, but I think he can definitely clear 40 yards.

Kalif Raymond OVER 23.5 Receiving Yards -113

Raymond has easily cleared this number in the first two games. While it’s a wild card to know where Keenum is going to go with the ball, I think Keenum knows what a “coach’s best friend” Raymond is, and since Keenum is practically a coach himself, he will look for Raymond a few times to secure the ball when they need to move the chains. He can go to Raymond short and let him work with the ball in his hands, and I think there’s no reason he isn’t up over 40 yards again.

Dontayvion Wicks OVER 41.5 Receiving Yards -113

The Bears offense is certainly more of a question this week, so it’s worth looking over on the other side of the aisle for any intriguing plays and Wicks is one for me. Wicks has cleared 70 yards in each of the first two games of the season, and I certainly don’t trust the Bears secondary to be sticky in better conditions. Last week, the secondary play improved, but I’m going to need to see it on a clean field and in good conditions to truly believe in it. I think the conditions slowed down the Vikings’ passing attack more than the Bears did. Wicks feels like a guy that will slip behind Tyrique Stevenson once or twice for a decent gain and comfortably clear 41.5 this evening.

item.title: Bills defense steps up in Week 3 win over Chargers
item.description: After spending two games looking like an issue, the defense took a step forward on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
For two games, the Buffalo Bills’ offense looked unstoppable. Their defense, on the other hand, looked extremely porous, allowing 31 points in each of the team’s first two victories. That the offense was able to score 36 and 41 pints, respectively, in those games is really the only reason why we haven’t seen more concern about the team’s defensive output overall.

We’ve seen some criticism of the defense, both on this site and elsewhere, and that criticism has been warranted. “The Bills won’t be able to win shootouts every week,” those critics declared, and they were proven right perhaps even earlier than they expected to be.

The Bills weathered three first half turnovers on Sunday against the Los Angeles Chargers, somehow entering halftime in a 10-10 tie. With two more turnovers in the second half contributing to a 13-10 Chargers lead midway through the fourth quarter, it was fair to wonder whether or not this was Buffalo’s day to drop an ugly game. However, the offense woke up in that final quarter, scoring a pair of touchdowns just four minutes apart to turn that 13-10 deficit into a 24-13 lead with just over three minutes to play.

The Bills were only in a position for those touchdowns to matter because of the continued tough play of their defensive unit on Sunday. Buffalo’s offensive woes placed the defense in adverse situations time and again, and the stop unit weathered the storm. Three of Buffalo’s five turnovers came inside their own territory, but the defense stood tough.

Buffalo’s first turnover—on the game’s first play from scrimmage, no less—came on a James Cook fumble that Los Angeles recovered at the Buffalo 47-yard line. That turnover directly led to a touchdown. Buffalo’s seconds turnover came on an interception at the Bills’ 43-yard line, as safety Genesis Smith jumped a route and intercepted Josh Allen. That gifted the Chargers great field position, which they converted into a Cameron Dicker field goal and a 10-0 advantage.

Buffalo’s fifth turnover should have been the back-breaker. Allen was sacked, and on his way down, he fumbled at the Bills’ 28-yard line. The Chargers could have thrown three incomplete passes and been in great shape for a 45-yard field goal. They could have run the clock down and added a game-icing touchdown. Instead, they did the one thing that they couldn’t do: they gave the ball right back to Buffalo without scoring.

On third down and five from Buffalo’s 23-yard line, Justin Herbert tried to force a pass up the seam to Marquez Valdes-Scantling. C.J. Gardner-Johnson jumped the route, intercepted the pass, and returned it to the Buffalo 43-yard line. From there on, Buffalo’s offense ran 19 plays for 103 yards and two touchdowns over the course of their next two drives.

Buffalo’s defensive effort throughout the day was outstanding. They held the Chargers to just one touchdown despite gifting them five extra possessions via turnovers. While they allowed some longer drives in the early going, allowing Los Angeles to march 47 yards for a touchdown on their first possession, they held the Chargers out of the end zone on each of their three longest drives. Los Angeles had a 63-yard drive end in a missed field goal, and then had a pair of 69-yard drives end in made field goals for Cameron Dicker.

This was a continuation of a trend that has shown itself this year, as Buffalo’s defense has stepped up in the biggest moments thus far. Even on Sunday, the Bills’ defense bowed its neck and gave the offense a chance to redeem itself in that fourth quarter. After Allen’s fumble, the Chargers ran eight plays on their next two drives. They gained a total of seventeen yards, threw one interception, and turned over the ball on downs. Those two turnovers directly led to Buffalo’s 14 second-half points, which gave them the margin needed to win the game.

Yes, there were still warts on defense. Some ugly penalties extended drives that should have ended. There’s also the necessary caveat that the Chargers aren’t exactly an offensive juggernaut, as they have totaled just 44 points this season and average just 309 yards per game. That average is way up from their first two weeks thanks to the 348 total yards they gained on Sunday.

Has Buffalo’s defense been perfect this year? No, it hasn’t been. However, after looking like it could be a huge liability through two games, Sunday’s effort was another step in the right direction for defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s charges. While they won’t play struggling offenses like Los Angeles every week, the Buffalo defense continued its trend of stepping up for the team in the biggest moments.

And, at least for one week, the offense can thank the defense for covering its mistakes rather than the reverse being true.

item.title: Jaycee Horn out indefinitely with torn quad
item.description: The Carolina Panthers are losing their star corner for an extended period of time.
item.content:encoded:
According to NFL news breaker Ian Rapaport, Carolina Panthers cornerback Jaycee Horn is out indefinitely with a torn quad.

Rapaport notes in his tweet that Horn is going to get multiple opinions, but injuries of this severity are almost always multi-month recoveries, especially if it’s a full tear. If it’s not a complete tear and more of a strain, Horn could avoid surgery and be back before a the end of the season. That said, the way this has been reported does not seem promising.

Horn has established himself as one of the best corners in the game and had started to shake the injury prone label after missing a total of just three games in the two seasons prior to this one. Now he’ll be headed back to injured reserve, and the Panthers will have to try to make do without him. His running mate Mike Jackson is also dealing with a groin injury, so it might get really ugly in the secondary for the next few weeks at least.

item.title: J.J. McCarthy joins the NFC East
item.description: The Giants have a new QB.
item.content:encoded:
There’s a new quarterback in the NFC East.

In the aftermath of Jaxson Dart suffering a season-ending injury last week, the New York Giants have reportedly acquired J.J. McCarthy in a trade with Minnesota Vikings.

McCarthy has become a meme (quite literally) since his NFL career hasn’t gone well for him thus far. The No. 10 overall pick from the 2024 NFL Draft missed his entire rookie season due to injury before throwing 11 touchdowns to 12 interceptions for a 72.6 passer rating last year.

With the Vikings adding Kyler Murray and re-signing Carson Wentz, McCarthy’s struggles dropped him to being Minnesota’ third quarterback option. Not great.

From an optics standpoint, I can get why people think it’s funny for the Giants to trade for him as it relates to any improbable effort to help keep their season alive.

But I don’t think this is a bad trade for the G-Men.

What’s the downside? Giving up a 2027 fifth-round pick? They already were projected to have two of them in that round so they still have one.

McCarthy, who turns 24 in January, probably stinks. He might not even get on the field ahead of Jameis Winston?

But McCarthy is probably better than Jake Haener, who was QB2 in Week 3. And if the Giants reach a point later this season where they’re eliminated, there’s really nothing to learn from playing Winston. They could look to play McCarthy and hope he shows some potential, either as a future option for them (backup or otherwise) or a potential trade piece in the offseason. McCarthy is under contract for the 2027 season.

Unless Winston gets hurt or egregiously struggles, I’m guessing the Philadelphia Eagles won’t see McCarthy when the Birds face the Giants in Week 9. But maybe he’ll be starting by the time the Eagles take on the Giants again in Week 18.

item.title: Sunday Aftermath: Week 3 injury apocalypse, J.J. McCarthy trade, and much more
item.description: Breaking down all of the NFL's biggest Week 3 storylines, including De'Von Achane's season-ending torn ACL.
item.content:encoded:
I bet on De’Von Achane’s talent in summer fantasy drafts. It wasn’t going well. Things just got a whole lot worse. Achane, who managed to appear in 44 of a possible 51 games his first three years in the league despite his pint size, suffered a torn ACL in Sunday’s loss to the Chiefs. It wasn’t because he was small and took a big hit. It was because he planted his right foot weird. So are the vagaries of football and the indignities of fantasy.

I was already “wrong” about Achane this season. I thought he was too good to wallow in RB2 territory despite the Dolphins’ severe offensive limitations. Wallow he very much did in Weeks 1 and 2. That didn’t feel great. This feels so much worse. Achane is an underdog story who cut against the unfounded “injury prone” concerns and played fantasy football the right way — aka lots of big plays and touchdowns. There was no scamming to his profile.

Now we don’t know if he will ever be the same. Turning 25 next month, Achane indeed wasn’t injury prone but is now very much injured. Can a player with his profile — small and explosive — survive the loss of any of his athleticism? 2-3 percent might not matter a whole lot if you’re Derrick Henry or Adrian Peterson. But 5-foot-9 and under 200 pounds?

There is some anecdotal hope in the past. 25-year-old Jamaal Charles tore his ACL in Week 2 2011. He was back the following Week 1 and rushed for a career-high 1,509 yards that season. There’s no need for things to be “over” for Achane. Just extended this offseason, his place in the Dolphins’ hierarchy is secure. He will be back. Hopefully he will be the same.

In his 2026 absence are Ollie Gordon II and Jaylen Wright, the latter of whom is currently week to week with a foot injury. Heading into the season, I thought any post-Achane committee would likely consist of Wright carrying the mail and Gordon changing the pace. Gordon briefly began the 2025 campaign ahead of Wright before the slightly older back easily overtook him. Now it’s Gordon in the driver’s seat after he handled 20 Week 3 touches in Wright’s absence.

A good start, but the Dolphins are not going to be hunting for one-back solutions. Both players will get the football. With only slim leads to go on, Gordon’s current better health and sizable Week 3 workload make him the preferred waivers option. Just be sure to get in some bids on Wright, too.

Five Week 3 Storylines

Baker Mayfield’s season goes from bad to worse with dislocated thumb. Mayfield’s third straight dud was by far his worst and most painful. Even before his end-of-game injury, Mayfield was having a miserable day at the office. Six sacks. A 50.0 completion percentage. Miscommunications with Emeka Egbuka. Just an “all of the above” rough performance. Now he’s reportedly going to have 2-4 weeks to clear his thoughts, though it could be longer with a quarterback throwing hand injury. Despite Mayfield’s cellar-dwelling play, it’s awful news for Egbuka and company. Mayfield’s backup is somehow 23-year-old rookie undrafted free agent Jalon Daniels. In other words, a move might be in order. Perhaps Jake Browning will be re-signed. With accuracy and decision-making two of Daniels’ pre-draft question marks, things probably will somehow get worse in Tampa.  

Mike Evans carted off with scary rib issue. If it was a bad day for the Bucs, the same was true for one of their former pirates. Evans suffered some sort of mid-section calamity, with the team announcing it as a rib injury but saying it might be his oblique. Whatever it was required the assistance of a cart, and might finally be the ailment that costs Evans some regular season time. Already dealing with a hip problem, Evans had quad and “abductor” concerns during camp. This is a 33-year-old who missed nine games last season. Relying on him was always a bit of a long shot. Left in his wake would be one of the league’s most undermanned skill corps, with some combination of Jacob Cowing, KhaDarel Hodge and Jordan Watkins trying to help out Deebo Samuel and George Kittle.  

Breece Hall part of the Week 3 injury parade. Bad: Hall injured his thigh. Worse: Head coach Aaron Glenn said he will not update the situation before Wednesday’s injury report. Hopefully the national media can fill in the blanks between now and Tuesday evening’s waivers run, but it not, fantasy managers will be left blindly bidding on Braelon Allen as either a potential league-winner or RB4 bench stash. There will probably be some in between, as Hall seems likely to miss at least a game or two. In NFL parlance, “thigh” usually means “the worst bruise you’ve ever seen,” It’s also possible Hall has some sort of quad injury. We are in an information vacuum, but proceed as if Hall will miss time.

Justin Jefferson goes down with ankle injury. The injury news is getting better as we go. Although Jefferson never returned against the Bucs after departing in the second quarter, head coach Kevin O’Connell claimed afterward he was “close” to doing so. That leaves hope that Jefferson’s sprain is not the highest anyone has ever seen and that he might actually take the field in Week 4. If he does, it will be in a (hopefully) newly functional attack with Kyler Murray under center vs. the league’s very worst team in the Dolphins. If he doesn’t, it will be a major missed opportunity in fantasy, but likely only a 1-2 game absence.

Jeremiyah Love commences takeover of Cardinals’ backfield. Limited to just 41.6 percent of the Cardinals’ snaps through their first two games, Love saw that number shoot up to 64.4 percent in San Francisco. He out-touched Tyler Allgeier 26-6 and out-gained him 109-9 as the Cardinals mounted a furious comeback. That “furious comeback” could be why Love was so much more involved than Weeks 1 and 2, but then again, Week 2 was also comeback game script. Allgeier has not been fully mothballed or even particularly close to it — he played 31 snaps against the 49ers — but the Cardinals are finally letting logic take over after using the No. 3 overall pick on Love.

Don't forget, for the latest on everything NFL, check out Rotoworld’s Player News, or follow @Rotoworld_FB or @RotoPat on Twitter/Bluesky.

Five More 3 Storylines

The Drake Maye situation spirals further out of control. And “situation” it is. Last year’s “MVP runner-up” is producing negative EPA per play. He has one touchdown compared to seven turnovers. He is not running effectively. He has taken at least three sacks all three starts. He is doing nothing well and the cavalry is not coming in relief. A.J. Brown is out at least two more games. This offensive line is not blocking. The offensive coordinator is not calling good plays. Quite literally nothing is going right, and until at least one thing does, fantasy managers can no longer even consider Maye in the top 12, even for dates like this week’s Bills road trip that we would typically regard as a shootout waiting to happen. That being said, for the dead-enders out there, the “bookmakers” have still somewhat improbably set the initial over/under at 48.5.

Dolphins rookie Chris Bell looks like a dude vs. the Chiefs. The news wasn’t all bad in Miami. With fellow rookie Caleb Douglas sidelined with an ankle injury, size/speed third-round prospect Bell finally got a chance to show what he could do, and boy was it something. Although he caught “just” four balls for 67 yards, he looked like a load in the open field. His breakaway speed was also on full display. Bell was separating. Now, considering the state of this offensive environment, it could be another month before Bell either matches or exceeds this performance. But it was enough to confirm his health following last year’s torn ACL, and to make him worth a waivers stab as the rare mid-season receiver addition who might actually make a difference.  

Seahawks’ backfield devolves into a committee. Limited to six touches due in part to a lost first half fumble, Jadarian Price had by far the worst performance of his young career. That’s extra bad since the first two weren’t exactly good. Disappointing though they have been, they are even more concerning than you might realize. Because even though young players struggle early all the time before hitting their stride and producing in the second half of the season, Price might not have that luxury. That’s because an ACL-rehabbing Zach Charbonnet has only one more required game on injured reserve. Maybe it will be more, but Price’s first few games weren’t just about being good. They were about distancing himself from his veteran teammate. He has failed to do so, and as a result, the hoped-for RB2 returns might never really materialize.

Marvin Harrison Jr. fails in three straight different game environments. As is the case with Price, it’s not just that Harrison is struggling. It’s the context in which he has done so. The Cardinals played ball-control offense in their Week 1 upset of the Chargers. Harrison caught one pass. They gobbled up garbage time against the Seahawks in Week 2. Marv was held without a reception. They furiously tried to come back in Week 3 against the 49ers. MHJ was limited to 3/40 on five targets. That that was his good line this season also speaks volumes, but what in these first three weeks and game environments suggest a corner is about to be turned? There is always Harrison’s theoretical talent, but that’s no longer a sound bet in Year 3. This is now about production, and Harrison just hasn’t had it.  

Brock Bowers is who we thought he was in season debut. Bowers’ Week 1 rug pull was amongst the most painful in recent memory. Somewhat shockingly, the damage was contained. The optimistic return timeline held. And the return actually went according to plan. A man amongst boys vs. the Saints, Bowers was also a wide receiver amongst tight ends. New coach Klint Kubiak isn’t pretending Bowers is something he’s not. He’s not griping about his run blocking. He’s just feeding him targets and Bowers is obliging with monster statlines. Not to get ahead of myself with the plural. This was one game. But that’s also how every game looks when Bowers is healthy. He never really was in 2025. Against all odds, he is now. He will carry your fantasy team for however long he can stay on the field.

Bonus Topic of the Week: The Giants acquire J.J. McCarthy for a fifth-round pick. This is the rare fantasy situation where everything speaks for itself. Jaxson Dart fill-in Jameis Winston doesn’t look like he can play anymore. McCarthy has never looked like he could play. That’s how a player just two years out from being a top-10 pick went for a fifth-rounder. McCarthy will almost certainly start for the G-Men at some point, but it will require a 3-4 week ramp-up period, and even then, the returns might not necessarily be better than Winston’s. Everyone deserves a second chance. McCarthy’s Vikings tenure had turned toxic. But with byes approaching and injuries mounting, McCarthy is not worth a speculative add in superflex leagues.  

Questions

1. I don’t get it — do the Rams not have enough tight ends?

2. So yeah, for real, what was Pete Carroll doing out there in 2025?

3. Do the Cowboys ever get tired?

Early Waivers Look (Players rostered in less than 50 percent of Yahoo leagues)

QB: Sam Darnold (vs. LAC), Kirk Cousins (vs. KC), Geno Smith (@CHI), Michael Penix Jr. (@NO), Marcus Mariota (vs. IND), Daniel Jones (@WAS)
RB: Braelon Allen, Ollie Gordon II, Jaylen Wright, Keaton Mitchell, Brian Robinson Jr., Tyler Allgeier, Kaleb Johnson
WR: Adonai Mitchell, Chris Bell, Malik Washington, Tre Harris, Mack Hollins, Jakobi Meyers
TE: Kenyon Sadiq, AJ Barner, T.J. Hockenson, Brenton Strange, Darren Waller
