item.description: We're going over what should be a lengthy NFL injury report for fantasy football managers in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
It never gets any easier for fantasy football managers. It feels like we've seen an abnormal amount of injured players through three weeks of the 2026 NFL season. Not that we're keeping track or anything (we are). Last week, QBs were the big storyline as Caleb Williams, Jaxson Dart and Jayden Daniels went down. This week, it was skill position players and lineup mainstays De'Von Achane, Justin Jefferson and Breece Hall who were hurt (among others). Let's go over the injury report and what to do if you have some key injured players in fantasy.

Week 4 NFL Injury Report

Quarterback

  • Caleb Williams, CHI (hamstring)

  • Jayden Daniels, WAS (elbow) — Out

  • Jaxson Dart, NYG (knee) — Out for season

  • Baker Mayfield, TB (thumb) — Out three weeks

Mayfield: Just when we thought we were clear of any new QB injuries … Mayfield left Sunday's loss to the Vikings with a dislocated right thumb. Head coach Todd Bowles told reporters on Monday that Mayfield will miss three weeks. That would put the QB in line to return in Week 7 vs. the Panthers. Jalon Daniels came in late in relief and he will get the first crack to replace Mayfield. Tampa Bay could also explore outside options as well if Mayfield is out long-term. Either way, this is a big downgrade for what was already a struggling Bucs passing game. It'll be difficult to trust players like Emeka Egbuka, Chris Godwin Jr. and Bucky Irving in fantasy.

Running Back

  • De'Von Achane, MIA (torn ACL) — Out for season

  • Breece Hall, NYJ (thigh)

  • Rico Dowdle, PIT (toe)

  • Travis Etienne Jr., NO (hamstring)

Achane: Miami lost its top running back early in the loss to the Chiefs on Sunday. And the worst was reported by ESPN Monday morning with Achane suffering a torn ACL, ending his 2026 season. Miami was already trending toward being one of the bottom-dwellers of the NFL and fantasy world this season. Losing Achane is the worst-possible scenario. With Achane sidelined, you can't really replace the type of player he is and that type of early-round draft capital. Ollie Gordon II will get the first crack to be RB1 with Jaylen Wright inactive against Kansas City. If you have Achane on your roster, your top waiver priority this week should be Gordon.

Hall: It's a thigh injury for Hall, who was tackled awkwardly late in the loss to Detroit. We'll have to monitor Hall's status at practice this week ahead of Week 4's meeting with the Bears. If Hall misses the next game, Braelon Allen figures to get the bulk of the work out of the backfield, and is another solid waiver wire target this week. Isaiah Davis could be a target in deeper formats.

Etienne: It had been a underwhelming start to Etienne's tenure in New Orleans. This is just more bad in a sea of bad. To make matters worse, Etienne was having an OK game before exiting against the Raiders in Week 3. He had 15 touches (including two catches) and 70 total yards — not bad production with room for more. Tyler Shough also threw four TDs to tight ends in the red zone, so one of those TDs could have gone to Etienne in another universe. Alas, now he's on the mend. We'll need more info and to see how practice goes this week as Minnesota preps for a game against the Dolphins in Week 4. If Jefferson is out, Jordan Addison becomes an attractive start. He had a 5-90-1 line for the Vikings against Tampa Bay. The matchup against Miami is juicy but the passing game could be limited given what we saw from Kyler Murray.

Nacua: The star wide receiver missed a second straight game with groin and hip issues. The team believes it's possible Nacua will be back in Week 4, per ESPN's Adam Schefter. With that said, it's still possible Nacua could undergo surgery on his groin. If the wideout doesn't show improvement, a procedure would be the next option. The team, however, does not believe Nacua needs to have surgery to correct the issue.

item.title: Davante Adams: 1-2 start is "nothing to freak out about"
item.description: When Davante Adams was a rookie on the Packers — way back in 2014 — the team got off to a 1-2 start.
item.content:encoded:
When Davante Adams was a rookie on the Packers — way back in 2014 — the team got off to a 1-2 start.

Green Bay’s quarterback then famously spelled out a word during a radio interview: “R-E-L-A-X.”

Eventually, that Packers team went 12-4 in the regular season, beat the Cowboys in the divisional round, and lost a wild NFC Championship game to the Seahawks.

It’s over a decade later, but perhaps that was somewhere in the back of Adams’ mind on Sunday night after the Rams lost to the Broncos, dropping Los Angeles’ record to 1-2.

“Stay in, I mean, it’s nothing to freak out about,” Adams said, via transcript from the Broncos, when asked about the team’s 1-2 start. “There’s a lot of football left, and it’s not like we’re not playing good ball, obviously excluding that first game.

“Unfortunately, I mean, I don’t know if it’s unfortunate, but based on our situation, unfortunately, this league is about wins and losses, so there’s a lot that we can take from a game like this and feel good about. But there’s no moral victories, so we’re definitely disappointed to not finish it out. But just to get back to what we do, and that’s going back to practice, get back to the drawing board and just find a way to finish off something again.”

With Puka Nacua sidelined for the last couple of weeks due to injury, Adams has been the team’s top receiving option — recording back-to-back games of 100 yards for the first time since joining the team last offseason.

While Nacua may be back for Week 4, the schedule will not get any easier, as the Rams will travel across the country to face the Eagles on Sunday.

item.title: J.J. McCarthy trade grades for Giants, Vikings after QB goes to New York for draft pick
item.description: Let’s hand out some grades for the Giants-Vikings trade involving J.J. McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
J.J. McCarthy is heading to the New York Giants.

A week after the franchise lost Jaxson Dart for hte season due to a knee injury that requires surgery, the Giants have sent an unconditional fifth-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft to the Minnesota Vikings for McCarthy, who lost training camp battles over the summer not just for the starting job (to Kyler Murray) but eventually for the backup job to Carson Wentz.

When Dart went down for the season, it sparked speculation that the Giants might swing a move for a new quarterback, rather than hand the keys to Jameis Winston for the entire season. While New York managed a win on Sunday against the 12-7 Tennessee Titans, the offense has not exactly been running on all cylinders after Dart’s injury. And with New York losing Brian Burns for the season due to a knee injury of his own, the Giants need every bit of offense they can get.

Let’s hand out some grades.

New York Giants: A-

After Dart’s injury, we tested the quarterback trade waters on the NFL Feed by asking which backup quarterbacks could be traded ahead of the annual NFL Trade Deadline.

While many dismissed the idea of a trade, given the risk associated with trading away a backup at a premium position, the Giants managed to swing a deal to acquire McCarthy well ahead of the deadline. Giving up a fifth-round pick for a cost-controlled quarterback that has ten NFL starts under his belt and is just 23 years old seems like a solid bit of business, even if it is your proverbial “dart throw.” While McCarthy has not lived up to the expectations with being a first-round selection, there is upside, and New York offensive coordinator Matt Nagy does have a history of quarterback development, dating back to his time with Mitchell Trubisky and the Chicago Bears. While Trubisky never lived up to the billing that came with being the No. 2 quarterback taken in the 2017 NFL Draft — eight spots ahead of Patrick Mahomes — Nagy was able to get Trubisky and the Bears to the playoffs.

If he can work similar magic during a season where the Giants lost their starter? Fantastic.

If not, New York gave up a fifth-round pick.

Minnesota Vikings: A

For the Vikings, this trade solves two distinct issues.

First, it ends the speculation over McCarthy’s future and eliminates any true chance of a quarterback controversy, at least for this season. When a team drafts a young quarterback in the first round, there is every expectation that the player will see the field. Even when you bring in a veteran like Murray.

After just three weeks, the Vikings are 3-0 and atop the NFC North. While Murray has not been flawless, the defense has been, as Brian Flores’ unit has flustered Jordan Love, Caleb Williams, and Baker Mayfield over the last three weeks. The Minnesota defense has given up 13.7 points per game — ranking second in the NFL — and when you look at Expected Points Added, the Vikings are almost off the chart:

Data from RBSDM.com.

This is a playoff defense that just needs some consistency from the offense, and with the talent around the quarterback position, a steady veteran might be the better answer for 2026 than the unpredictability McCarthy has shown over his ten NFL starts.

The other reason this is a win for Minnesota is a financial one. By trading McCarthy, even on his rookie deal, the move saves the Vikings some money. As noted by Tom Pelissero, by moving the quarterback now the Vikings save nearly $5 million on cash and cap space:

That is also a good bit of business for a quarterback that likely needs a fresh start.

Speaking of which …

J.J. McCarthy: A

This is good for J.J. McCarthy as well.

Things just did not come together for him in Minnesota. There were flashes — like a comeback win over the Chicago Bears at the start of last season — but it never truly clicked for him with the Vikings.

Sometimes, you just need a fresh start.

He will get that, playing for John Harbaugh. He may not start right away for the Giants, it is likely he gets some time to learn Nagy’s system, but this could be a good environment for him to showcase what he could be in the NFL. With Dart on the roster, it is unlikely that McCarthy supplants the other young quarterback on the roster as the starting QB going forward, but this could be the best chance for McCarthy to earn another starting job elsewhere in the league.

item.title: How long is Baker Mayfield out? Latest updates on Buccaneers QB's thumb injury
item.description: Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield suffered a dislocated thumb in Week 3 against the Vikings. How long will he be out because of the injury?
item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers lost 23-16 in their Week 3 game against the Minnesota Vikings, marking their third consecutive defeat to open the 2026 NFL season.

That said, Tampa Bay's bigger loss during the game was that of its starting quarterback Baker Mayfield, who exited the game late with a thumb injury.

Mayfield was injured on the Buccaneers' penultimate drive and was unable to return to the game. Now, it looks like he is in legitimate danger of missing his first start with Tampa Bay after starting 57 consecutive games, postseason included, since signing with the franchise ahead of the 2023 NFL season.

Here's everything to know about Mayfield's injury and when he may return to the field for the Buccaneers.

How long is Baker Mayfield out?

Buccaneers head coach Todd Bowles said Mayfield will miss "a minimum of three weeks" with the injury, seemingly avoiding an IR stint. According to multiple reports, an MRI revealed no fracture and no ligament or tendon damage to the thumb.

What happened to Baker Mayfield?

Mayfield suffered a dislocated thumb injury in the Buccaneers' Week 3 game against the Vikings.

Mayfield's injury occurred during a fourth-and-13 play late in the fourth quarter. He was desperately scrambling back in the hopes of an open receiver but failed to do so as three Vikings converged on him.

Mayfield was able to get off a last-ditch heave that fell incomplete well short of the line to gain, but he hit his right thumb hard against Vikings linebacker Blake Cashman on the play. The 31-year-old quarterback's thumb bent awkwardly as a result of that contact, and he immediately doubled over in pain, grabbing at his throwing hand.

Below is a full look at the play that left Mayfield injured.

item.title: 5 takeaways from the Steelers’ 30-27 win over the Cincinnati Bengals
item.description: Takeaways, overreactions and analysis from the Steelers’ Week 3 win.
item.content:encoded:
And just like that, the Steelers aren’t bad again. Following a listless performance on offense in Week 2, Pittsburgh won a shootout over the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 3 .

As always, there are plenty of takeaways to be had.

1. Steelers show resiliency

Following last week’s ugly defeat at the hands of the New England Patriots, I wrote that I wanted to see how the Steelers would respond to a loss under the team’s new coaching staff.

It’s safe to say the team made the right adjustments under head coach Mike McCarthy.

After a horribly incompetent Week 2 on offense, the Steelers dropped 30 points on a Bengals defense that has been surprisingly solid to open the season. That’s not to say it was a perfect showing, but it was a far cry from the unit’s multi-level failures last week.

“Resiliency is critical to any type of success, whether it’s playing one division game or overcoming a loss last week.” McCarthy said postgame. “Momentum is a huge part of our game. It’s a hard-working football team. … Once you get through the first of everything as a team, there’s usually bumps that you go through, so, they’ve stayed the course.”

While the Patriots loss was an abnormally bad game, it’s fair to say that there was always going to be some turbulence early in the McCarthy era as Pittsburgh adjusted to its first new head coach since 2007. The ride has indeed been bumpy through three games, but the team showed the poise to not let a disaster last week spiral out of control.

It’s still difficult to get a read on the 2026 Steelers. But given the improvement this week from the last, that’s a good problem to have at the moment.

2. The offensive line shows up

One of the through lines of last week’s loss was how thoroughly Pittsburgh’s offensive front was dominated by the Patriots’ defensive line. Not one player in Pittsburgh’s starting five had a good game.

But despite playing against an improved Cincinnati front on Sunday led by all-world nose tackle Dexter Lawrence, the Steelers’ offensive line was largely fantastic in both the run and pass game. Pittsburgh averaged an impressive six yards per rush, while quarterback Aaron Rodgers was sacked only twice — once on a blitz pickup miscommunication, and another on an extended play.

Of course, Pittsburgh’s sudden success in this area of the game clearly correlates with a significant change this week, swapping out right tackle Dylan Cook and right guard Spencer Anderson for first-round rookie Max Iheanachor and veteran backup Brock Hoffman, respectively.

While I wasn’t able to keep an eye on him on every play, Iheanachor seemed to have a stellar debut. His easy athleticism shines in his mirroring in pass protection and explosion off the ball as a run blocker. His initial charting backed the eye test — according to New Gen Stats, he only allowed three pressures on 36 pass-blocking reps, including a 75% one-on-one rate.

At guard, Hoffman’s first Steelers start might not have been as flashy, but he still put together a key performance limiting Lawrence’s impact alongside Zach Frazier and Mason McCormick. Despite having two new names on the line, it was the most coordinated the group has looked all season by a mile.

And the strong pass protection numbers weren’t juiced by an exceptionally fast time to throw by Rodgers, either. In fact, according to ESPN’s Benjamin Solak, Rodgers’ 3.19-second average time to throw on Sunday was the longest of his Steelers career.

The Pittsburgh offensive line finally clicking with Iheanachor in the lineup was great news, not just in the context of the Bengals’ game, but for the long-term prospects of a team that has spent heavy resources trying to rebuild the group in recent seasons. There’s still a lot of football to be played before sweeping pronouncements, of course, but the Steelers’ offensive line looked promising on Sunday.

3. Jaylen Warren is RB1

OK, maybe Jaylen Warren played a little bit too much on Sunday, given his legs were the only thing stopping him by the time the fourth quarter rolled around.

But overall, Warren’s performance in Week 3 showed exactly why he should be getting a larger workload moving forward. Against the Bengals, he finished with 127 rushing yards and a 7.5-yard average, not including an 87-yard run that was taken back due to a questionable holding call.

And in the passing game, Warren added another 49 receiving yards, and continued to shine as a pass protector.

As those long runs showed, Warren’s long speed isn’t enough to take every big break to the house, but his burst and contact balance remain excellent. He’s an every-down threat who continues to deserve more playing time than he’s usually given.

Warren remains one of the NFL’s most underrated running backs. He’s also clearly been the Steelers’ best and most consistent skill position player through three weeks. Sunday finally showed what he can do in a bell-cow role.

4. The defense could’ve used Joey Porter Jr.

Despite giving up 27 points on Sunday, I’m far from worried about the Steelers defense. The Joe Burrow/Ja’Marr Chase/Tee Higgins/Chase Brown attack was going to be better than anything Pittsburgh had faced up to that point in the season, and sure enough, that elite offensive core made some elite plays on Sunday.

If there’s anything to be slightly perturbed by, it should be the Steelers’ pass rush not making much of an impact until later in the game, only sacking Burrow once. Still, Pittsburgh’s edge room is made up of proven players, and having receivers who get open with the ease of Chase and Higgins remains a great antidote to pressure.

And those pass catchers might’ve been better minimized if the Steelers had their best cover corner available on Sunday.

Pittsburgh clearly didn’t trust its defensive backs in man coverage against the Bengals’ star duo, but instead, Burrow picked them apart in zone. Asante Samuel Jr. put together a respectable effort matching up against Higgins, but clearly couldn’t match the latter’s size and contested catch ability. Samuel was eventually benched for rookie Daylen Everette, who has more traditional boundary corner size.

Porter would’ve given the Steelers a bigger presence at corner to match up with Higgins, and his press-man speciality, along with Jamel Dean, would’ve allowed the team to switch up more coverage concepts. Ultimately, the Steelers will want Porter down the line if they want the defense to live up to its potential this season, and the star corner has said he’ll “definitely” play at some point — whatever that means.

Of course, it’ll be interesting to see what Porter’s return timeline looks like as the Steelers enter a short week ahead of a matchup against the Cleveland Browns.

5. Odds and ends

  • Sample sizes are a funny thing. In two of the Steelers’ three games so far this season, Rodgers has largely played well and done a better job pushing the ball downfield and extending plays than he did in most of 2025. It’ll be interesting what the trend looks like over the rest of the season.
  • Ben Skowronek caught a touchdown pass and recovered a key fumble when the Bengals muffed a punt. One of the most underrated Steelers had an underrated performance on Sunday.
  • For as impressive as Pittsburgh’s offense was on Sunday, there was still quite a bit of meat left on the bone in the passing game. The team’s performance against Cincinnati felt like the natural continuation of the promise the team showed against Atlanta in Week 1, but there’s still a lot of work to do.
  • Eli Heidenreich was an inactive on Sunday while both Lew Nichols and Travis Homer got a nod on the game day roster. This isn’t a knock on the rookie, who was never expected to be much of a contributor this season, but is interesting considering that he made the roster and the other two did not.
  • Pittsburgh has a problem with burning timeouts too early.
  • I continue to be perplexed by Roman Wilson. He was second on the team in receiving with 60 yards on Sunday (including a touchdown), but also dropped a pass that hit him in the hands, leading to a Bengals interception and eventual touchdown. The inconsistencies remain far too consistent.
  • Mike McCarthy might’ve lowered the “volume” of the Steelers’ game plan in practice this week, but his play design was consistently strong against the Bengals.
  • The Steelers relied a bit more on the more experienced left side of the offensive line on Sunday, but Warren saw success running all over the field on Sunday.
  • Cam Johnston’s 51-yard punt that was eventually muffed was an impressive one — I’m just happy he didn’t suffer another lower-body injury on the earlier running-into-the-punter penalty.
  • One of Metcalf’s two holding penalties is tough to really hold against him, but it did continue what’s been a rough start to the season for the Steelers’ top receiver. It’s good he caught a touchdown on Sunday.
  • Darnell Washington runs like he has a reputation to upkeep. And it keeps delivering entertaining results.
  • It was encouraging to see Derrick Harmon’s big, game-ending sack. He’s up to 1.5 over the first three weeks of the season, a good sign for a player who needed to show more as a pass rusher this season.
  • Patrick Queen was everywhere on Sunday with 13 total tackles. Another strong performance from one of Pittsburgh’s off-ball linebackers.
  • After a slow start to the season, the Steelers showed some potential as a legitimately entertaining team. Hopefully that trend continues.

Pittsburgh won’t have long to enjoy its narrative-changing win. The Steelers next take the field in Cleveland on Thursday Night Football in Week 4.

What are your takeaways from Steelers vs. Bengals? Agree/disagree with the ones above? Join the Behind the Steel Curtain community and let us know in the comments!

item.content:encoded:
Howdy, y’all. Back again for another look at which five Miami Hurricanes were good in a 52-3 win over Central Michigan in the eyes of Pro Football Focus, and which five were not.

As usual, going with a minimum of 20 snaps here to qualify.

Top 5 Canes

1) Darian Mensah – 91.8

2) Marquise Lightfoot – 89.8

3) Malachi Toney – 76.6

4) Ethan O’Connor – 76.1

5) Cam Pruitt – 74.7

Mensah and Toney should be on this list about every week, and I have to wonder if Toney got knocked for the offensive pass interference call on his freakish touchdown grab that was overturned. I see that push not called in just about every game, but it was here…..in what was frankly a terribly officiated game. Mensah, 23/27 338, three passing touchdowns, one rushing, no turnovers. What is there not to love?

Speaking of, despite the personal foul on the fumble return by Damon Wilson II, Lightfoot dominated and continues his breakout season. He was all over the place with two sacks and 2.5 tackles for loss, so yeah, that grade clearly meets the eye test.

O’Connor was sticky, allowing two catches for a grand total of three yards with three tackles and a pass break up. He’s playing an important role now, and he’s playing it well. Pruitt had one missed tackle credited to him, but he still led the team in tackles and allowed no catches on a target. So also, a nice game for him.

Bottom 5 Canes

1) Damon Wilson II – 54.7

2) Milan Parris – 55.8

3) Zechariah Poyser – 56.3

4) Omar Thornton – 59.0

5) JJ Dunnigan – 59.8

I wonder how much this would be different for Wilson if that fumble return touchdown that was wiped out by Lightfoot’s penalty would have counted. In any event, Miami’s important edge rusher had no tackles and two QB pressures. He also had a roughing the passer call on the first drive that facilitated . Miami needs more from him at Clemson on Saturday.

It feels like some nits were picked with Miami’s secondary, and I can’t say that I agree too wholeheartedly. CMU went 11 plays, 40 yards on their first drive for a field goal. They completed two short passes for three and four yards on that drive. That’s it. CMU had drives of three, three, three, five, and one yard the rest of the half against Miami’s starters. That’s close to perfect. Poyser was dinged for a pair of missed tackles, so perhaps I get that, but the rest? Eh, I just don’t. The defense largely played as it needed to absent perhaps a bit more pressure.

item.title: Vikings Trade J.J. McCarthy to New York Giants
item.description: An absolutely nonsensical trade
item.content:encoded:
Last week, I briefly talked about how the nonsensical trade rumors had started surrounding Minnesota Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy.

Today, as it turns out, the Vikings have decided to make a completely nonsensical trade.

Numerous sources are reporting that the Vikings are, in fact, trading McCarthy to the New York Giants. The return is, reportedly, a 2027 fifth-round draft choice.

So, the Vikings have decided to trade the highest-drafted quarterback in franchise history, a player they took with the #10 overall pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, after just ten NFL starts. This also puts the Vikings in a situation where they have no quarterbacks under contract for the 2027 season. Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz are both here on one-year deals.

Honestly, after watching that performance from Murray on Sunday and knowing the injury histories that both Murray and Wentz have, it boggles the mind that you would rather be two snaps from having your season rest on the right arm of Max Brosmer than potentially having J.J. McCarthy back there instead.

I’m sure that there will be plenty more on this in the coming days, but that’s the big story as it stands right now. The Vikings are, in fact, trading J.J. McCarthy to the New York Football Giants for, essentially, nothing.

Hooray.

item.title: One potential Mac Jones suitor is off the board after trading for J.J. McCarthy
item.description: The Giants have traded for J.J. McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero broke the news that the New York Giants are trading for Minnesota Vikings backup J.J. McCarthy.

Reports surfaced on Sunday that the Giants were interested in San Francisco 49ers quarterback Mac Jones, but there were three other quarterbacks: McCarthy, Jones, Jimmy Garoppolo, Justin Fields, and Gardner Minshew.

The Giants’ offensive coordinator, Matt Nagy, had a chance to select Jones in 2021 while coaching the Chicago Bears, but passed. He passed again on Jones, this time for another first-rounder who should never have been selected that high to begin with.

The Giants gave up a fifth-round pick for McCarthy, who was drafted in 2024. We’ll never know what the 49ers’ asking price is for Jones when he was on the hypothetical trade block last year, but we may find out if there are any other QB-needy teams during the next month and a half.

It’ll likely take an injury at the position, or a team that wasn’t a contender emerges. Until then, Jones remains on the 49ers’ roster.

item.title: Vikings send J.J. McCarthy to the Giants for a 2027 fifth-round pick
item.description: Minnesota send 10th pick in 2024 to New York.
item.content:encoded:
The J.J. McCarthy experiment in Minnesota has ended. In New York, it's just beginning.

Per multiple reports, the Vikings have traded the tenth overall pick in the 2024 draft to the Giants. In return, the Vikings will receive a 2027 fifth-round pick.

The Giants have a clear need at the position, given the knee injury that will keep Jaxson Dart out for at least the rest of the regular season. On Sunday, the starter was Jameis Winston, with Jake Haener as the understudy.

In Minnesota, McCarthy lost the starting job to Kyler Murray before falling behind Carson Wentz to the third spot on the depth chart. From the moment McCarthy was benched, it seemed that he was on borrowed time in Minnesota — even though everyone involved was saying all the right things.

For the Giants, the move brings the former Michigan quarterback (coached by Jim Harbaugh) to the NFL team coached by John Harbaugh.

For now, Winston is the starter. Whether McCarthy gets an opportunity to play depends on whether Winston is injured — and whether Winston remains sufficiently effective.

item.title: Giants trade for J.J. McCarthy, giving new life to QB buried on Vikings roster
item.description: The Giants made a major move to acquire QB talent after a season-ending injury to start Jaxson Dart.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants are wasting little time replenishing their quarterback depth chart.

A week after starter Jaxson Dart suffered a knee injury that will cost him at least the remainder of the regular season, the Giants have acquiredMinnesota Vikings backup J.J. McCarthy for a Day 3 pick in the 2027 NFL draft. Minnesota announced the deal Monday, Sept. 28, a day after starting quarterback Kyler Murray returned to the lineup and helped the Vikings run their record to 3-0. The transaction is pending until McCarthy passes a physical with the Giants.

McCarthy, 23, the tenth overall pick of the 2024 NFL Draft, had fallen to third on the Vikings' depth chart. He missed his entire rookie year with a meniscus injury and was inconsistent as a starter in 2025, though he wound up with a 6-4 record largely thanks to performances at the end of that season when the Vikings had already fallen out of playoff contention.

Minnesota signed Murray, the No. 1 overall pick (by the Arizona Cardinals) of the 2019 draft in the offseason, and he beat out McCarthy for the QB1 role before preseason games even started over the summer. Carson Wentz later secured the backup job and played in the first two regular-season games after Murray suffered a concussion early in Week 1.

The Giants won their first game without Dart, beating the winless Tennessee Titans 12-7 amid nor'easter conditions in the Meadowlands on Sunday. Newly promoted backup Jameis Winston had another uninspiring outing after struggling against the Los Angeles Rams, against whom Dart was injured one week ago. Winston completed 14 of 22 passes for 118 yards against Tennessee. The Giants opted for a run-heavy game plan (33 attempts) given the challenging weather but have yet to score a touchdown since Dart was injured in L.A. They will host the Arizona Cardinals in Week 4.

First-year Giants head coach John Harbaugh said last week that "all options are open" regarding the team's approach behind center after he finally admitted Dart likely wouldn't be back this season.

J.J. McCarthy-Harbaugh connection

McCarthy rose to prominence while leading the University of Michigan to a national championship during the 2023 season while playing for Jim Harbaugh, John's younger brother. McCarthy went 27-1 as the Wolverines' starter, his only loss coming at the end of the 2022 campaign, when Michigan fell to Texas Christian University in the College Football Playoff semifinals.

Jim Harbaugh, who returned to the NFL immediately after Michigan won its title, talked glowingly of McCarthy prior to the 2024 draft but was never going to bring him to the Los Angeles Chargers, who already had a young superstar (Justin Herbert) at the position.

"I think he plays quarterback the best of any quarterback in the draft," Jim Harbaugh said at the time. "He's incredible. So, big market, small market. Cold weather, hot weather, it won't matter."

McCarthy was a bit of a conundrum to assess prior to that draft. His mobility, arm strength and gaudy record all worked in his favor, but he was surrounded by scads of NFL-caliber talent in Ann Arbor and rarely had to perform heroically in high-leverage situations for the Wolverines.

J.J. McCarthy draft pick compensation

The Vikings will receive a fifth-round pick in the 2027 draft from the Giants in exchange for McCarthy.

J.J. McCarthy contract status

McCarthy's rookie contract is worth a fully guaranteed $21.9 million over the first four years of his career. His base salary this season is only $836,000. The Giants will have to decide next year whether to pick up McCarthy's fifth-year option for the 2028, also a fully-secured balloon payment available to former first-round picks. If the Giants decline the option, McCarthy would become a free agent in 2028.

Minnesota Vikings QB depth chart

▶ QB1 Kyler Murray

▶ QB2 Carson Wentz

▶ QB3 Max Brosmer (practice squad)

New York Giants QB depth chart

▶ QB1 Jameis Winston

▶ QB2 J.J. McCarthy

▶ QB3 Jake Haener

▶ Jaxson Dart (injured reserve)

item.title: Lions Week 3 snap counts: Breaking down defensive changes vs. Jets
item.description: Exploring the Detroit Lions’ defensive changes in Week 3 vs. Jets and why they made them.
item.content:encoded:
After starting the season 1-1 with glaring holes in defensive execution, the Detroit Lions made some significant changes to their personnel, some of which helped them get back on track, leading to a 31-24 win over the New York Jets in Week 3.

Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward.

Quarterback

  • Jared Goff: 65 (100%)
  • Josh Dobbs: Did Not Play

After a bumpy start to the game, Goff settled in quickly and continued his high level of play. While you’d like to see the offense sharp from start to finish, it’s hard to argue with the offense putting up 31 points in all three games so far this season.

Running back

  • Jahmyr Gibbs: 45 (69%)
  • Sione Vaki: 20 (31%) — 15 special teams snaps (65%)
  • Jacob Saylors: 2 (3%) — 15 (65%)

Gibbs was once again a human highlight reel in this game, but Aaron Glenn’s Jets exposed a possible weakness: pass protection. Glenn’s repeated A-gap blitzes were a problem for Gibbs, and likely why Vaki saw his snaps increase, as he was terrific in pass protection. Vaki’s ability to contribute in the run and pass game proved to teams that he’s not just a one-trick player that will tip the offensive play call.

Vaki talked with Pride of Detroit after the game and discussed his growth since the beginning of the season:

“The preparation going into these past two weeks, going out there and letting loose, and not being afraid to mess up. Being able to believe in myself, supported by (running backs) coach (Tashard) Choice and the boys in the room, has helped push me forward and has been a real confidence builder.”

Vaki went on to discuss how he tries to be the aggressor in pass protection:

“It’s definitely a conscious choice. Watching the film of (Jets) Demario Davis, being the great linebacker that he is, we knew he was going to try and run through our faces, and I just knew I had to respond by stuffing my face in there. There’s still some things to clean up, but today’s game did feel good.”

And for those worried that threatening the blitz could be a way for defenses to get Gibbs off the field, the Lions did respond by running some 21 personnel, with both Gibbs and Vaki on the field at the same time. A nice counterpunch by offensive coordinator Drew Petzing.

Wide receiver

  • Jameson Williams: 53 (82%)
  • Amon-Ra St. Brown: 48 (74%)
  • Isaac TeSlaa: 31 (48%)
  • Tay Martin: 2 (3%) — 15 (65%)
  • Tom Kennedy: 0 (0%) — 8 (35%)

With the Lions deploying some heavier sets against the Jets—13 personnel and Jumbo packages saw upticks in usage—the Lions wide receivers saw their opportunities scaled back a tick. Snap distribution remains very similar to past weeks, but it wouldn’t be surprising if this is St. Brown’s lowest snap count this season.

Tight end

  • Sam LaPorta: 60 (92%)
  • Brock Wright: 38 (58%) — 10 (43%)
  • Jackson Meeks: 10 (15%) — 2 (9%)
  • Tyler Conklin: DNP (INACTIVE)

As mentioned above, the Lions deployed a fair amount of 13 personnel in this game, with the wrinkle being that they split Meeks out wide to stretch the Jets’ Base defense. There will be games moving forward that the Lions will want a more balanced TE3 like Conklin on the field, but this new wrinkle with Meeks illustrates the versatility this group has.

Offensive line

  • LT Penei Sewell: 65 (100%)
  • LG Christian Mahogany: 65 (100%) — 5 (22%)
  • C Juice Scruggs: 65 (100%) — 5 (22%)
  • RG Tate Ratledge: 65 (100%) — 5 (22%)
  • RT Blake Miller: 65 (100%) — 5 (22%)
  • T Larry Borom: 15 (23%) — 5 (22%)
  • G/T Miles Frazier: 0 (0%) — 5 (22%)
  • C Seth McLaughlin: DNP
  • LG Ben Bartch: DNP (INJURED)

With their preferred starting five healthy again, the offensive line played very well in this game, slowing down a Jets defense near the top of all defensive rankings entering Week 3. Overall, the Lions gave up just eight pressures and two sacks, but the offensive line accounted for only five pressures and was not to blame for either sack.

As previously mentioned, the Lions leaned on their Jumbo sets in this game, utilizing Borom as a sixth offensive lineman for nearly a quarter of offensive snaps.

Interior defensive line

  • 3T Alim McNeill: 48 (73%) — 3 (13%)
  • 3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 33 (50%) — 2 (9%) — 1 offensive snap (2%)
  • DT Tyleik Williams: 30 (45%) — 3 (13%)
  • DL Levi Onwuzurike: 11 (17%)
  • 3T Mekhi Wingo: DNP (INACTIVE)

The defense made a lot of personnel adjustments in this game, with the first clear change being the scaling back of McNeill’s snaps. While 73% is still a big percentage, that’s about the spot he’s been at in the past when he’s been his most productive. His seven pressures and a sack illustrate this was a smart decision.

With McNeill scaling back a bit, that opened up the opportunities for his backup, rookie Skyler Gill-Howard, to increase his workload, and he rewarded them with three pressures and a half-sack (he split with Aidan Hutchinson).

Gill-Howard spoke with Pride of Detroit following the game and discussed his first NFL sack:

“The guard (Jordan Meridith), he was the second one because the first (Dylan Parham) got hurt—I knew I could beat him laterally, so that’s what I did; I took an inside counter, and while I got a little past the quarterback, the D-line did a good job of forcing him up, allowing me to spin out and get it—and of course, Hutch was right there.”

Gill-Howard also saw one snap on offense on a goal-line run that resulted in a Gibbs touchdown. Although the play went in the opposite direction of Gill-Howard’s block, it looks like a precursor to something the Lions could build on moving forward.

“You know coach (Dan) Campbell. You’ve seen those types of plays throughout his tenure here. He told me during training camp that he was going to put something in and we came up with ‘that’ for now, and we’ll see what happens in the future.”

EDGE

  • EDGE Aidan Hutchinson: 64 (97%) — 1 (4%)
  • Rush End DJ Wonnum: 44 (67%) — 3 (13%)
  • Big End Tyler Lacy: 19 (29%) — 5 (22%)
  • Rush End Derrick Moore: 9 (14%)
  • Rush End Eric O’Neill: 1 (2%) — 13 (57%)
  • Big End Ahmed Hassanein: DNP (INACTIVE)

While McNeill saw his reps scaled back a bit, the Lions ramped Hutchinson’s up, as he only took two defensive snaps off all game. Despite facing what looked like constant double teams, Hutchinson still managed five pressure and the half-sack mentioned above.

Typically, when the Lions deploy three-linebacker sets, they lean on a Big End (Tyler Lacy) to work opposite Hutchinson, but that wasn’t the case on Sunday. Wonnum saw his snaps increase in multiple formations beyond what we have seen from a rush end in the past. Wonnum also rewarded the team for the move, delivering three pressures and two sacks.

Linebacker

  • MIKE Jack Campbell: 66 (100%) — 3 (13%)
  • SAM Derrick Barnes: 57 (86%) — 1 (4%)
  • SAM Trevor Nowaske: 33 (50%) — 17 (74%)
  • WILL Malcolm Rodriguez: 19 (29%) — 7 (30%)
  • WILL Amen Ogbongbemiga: 0 (0%) — 17 (74%)
  • MIKE Jimmy Rolder: 0 (0%) — 15 (65%)
  • WILL Devin White: DNP (INACTIVE)

Campbell continues to play every defensive rep, and Barnes only misses a handful of snaps a game, but the LB3/4 spot saw a big shakeup in this game. White, previously in a starting role, was a healthy scratch, giving Rodriguez the start at WILL. However, the big change came with Nowaske, who was deployed all over the field and was on the field for half the game.

Pride of Detroit spoke with Nowaske after the game and asked him if his increased usage was opponent-specific, or something that was a result of his performances in practice and games.

“It could be a combination of both. I know I am a good linebacker in this league. I feel like I’ve done a good job in the preseason and when I’ve gotten my opportunities on defense. I was kind of used all over the field today, whether it was defensive end, OLB (SAM), inside backer, or nickel. Whenever I’m getting an opportunity, I want to make the most of it. I don’t ask too many questions; I just go out there and do my job.”

Nowaske made several key fourth-quarter stops, including tracking down Jets RB Breece Hall on a swing to the sideline and making a touchdown-saving tackle.

“It’s year four now, and the game is slowing down a ton for me,” Nowaske said. “So being able to dissect those plays and react a little bit faster is definitely helping me make more plays when I get those opportunities.”

Cornerback

  • NB/CB Roger McCreary: 64 (97%) — 3 (13%)
  • CB D.J. Reed: 62 (94%) — 1 (4%)
  • CB Ennis Rakestraw: 23 (35%) — 2 (9%)
  • CB Rock Ya-Sin: 13 (20%) — 13 (57%)
  • CB Khalil Dorsey: 0 (0%) — 12 (52%)
  • NB Keith Abney: 0 (0%) — 2 (9%)

The secondary saw some of the biggest changes as the Lions moved Ya-Sin to a reserve CB4 role and promoted McCreary to a starting role. McCreary not only started at CB2 on the outside, but also kicked inside when the team shifted to subpackage sets, bringing Rakestraw on to supplement outside snaps as CB3.

This group is still working through on-field and mental mistakes, but they did show some signs of improvement. It’ll take time to build communication in this scheme, but baby steps forward are better than continuing to regress.

One final note: while Abney didn’t see the field on defense, he was taking reps at free safety in warm-ups. It’s not entirely clear where he fits in the pecking order, but he could be the next man up at nickel (behind McCreary) and free safety (behind Chuck Clark).

Safety

  • S Chuck Clark: 66 (100%) — 3 (13%)
  • NB/S Christian Izien: 64 (97%) — 7 (30%)
  • S Jalen Mills: (%) — (%)
  • S Bishop Fitzgerald: DNP (INACTIVE)

With Avonte Maddox and Thomas Harper landing on injured reserve this week, the Lions shifted Izien from a starting nickel role to a starting strong safety role, the one typically occupied by Brian Branch. While this role demands an expansion of duties for Izien, it’s actually not too far off from what he did at nickel. He spent a lot of time in the box—where he’s at his best—and was used as a primary run gap filler and pass rusher, accounting for a team-leading 11 tackles (nine solo), including three tackles for loss and a pass deflection.

“I think my ‘box presence’ gets a lot of the credit, but I think I can be a well-rounded safety,” Izien said. “I believe I can play deep, even though my game has stood out more in the box.”

Clark also saw his role expand with the Lions’ short personnel at safety, and his game-sealing sack-fumble at the end of the game illustrated how important the veteran is to the Lions’ defense right now.

Specialists

  • K Jake Bates: 11 (48%)
  • P Jack Fox: 7 (30%)
  • LS Hogan Hatten: 7 (30%)

Steady improvement from this group, as they’re getting sharper by the week.

item.title: Giants trading for quarterback J.J. McCarthy
item.description: The Giants are trading for quarterback J.J. McCarthy, bolstering a QB room that has been reeling following the loss of Jaxson Dart for the regular season.
item.content:encoded:
The Giants are trading for Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy, bolstering a QB room that has been reeling following the loss of Jaxson Dart for the regular season.

New York is sending a fifth-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft to Minnesota.

McCarthy had been serving as the Vikings' No. 3 QB this season, behind Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz.

Joe Schoen and the Giants did legwork on McCarthy ahead of the 2024 NFL Draft (McCarthy went 10th overall), but picked Malik Nabers at No. 6 and waited until 2025 to select a franchise QB -- when they tabbed Dart at No. 25. 

McCarthy, 23, had a relatively rocky season for the Vikings in 2025, completing 140 of 243 passes (57.6 percent) for 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions, with Minnesota going 6-4 in his 10 starts. He also rushed 37 times for 181 yards and four touchdowns. 

McCarthy's season was also injury-riddled, with him missing five games due to a high ankle sprain suffered in Week 2, one game because of a concussion, and one game due to a hand injury. 

With the Giants adding McCarthy, he could eventually push Jameis Winston for the starting job. At the very least, he will be a higher upside backup option than Jake Haener, who served as the No. 2 QB on Sunday. 

And unlike Winston -- who is mostly a pocket passer -- McCarthy can make things happen with his legs.

Speaking after their Week 3 win, head coach John Harbaughsaid he expected Winston to be the starter in Week 4 regardless of who the team acquired, but did not elaborate further when it came to Winston's hold on the job.

Winston struggled badly in Week 2 against the Rams after being thrust into action following Dart's early injury, badly missing his receivers at times while going just 11-for-27 for 118 yards and throwing a bad interception in the red zone.

Winston was slightly better in New York's Week 3 victory over the Titans, completing 14 of 22 passes for 118 yards. While the rain and wind played a part in the gameplan on Sunday, and likely impacted some of Winston's throws, he continued to be off target more often than not. He also sat in the pocket for too long, and was sacked three times. 

In September, the Giants signed Winston to a two-year extension worth $13 million that takes him through the 2028 season.

McCarthy is under contract through 2027, with a fifth-year option for 2028.

item.title: Pass protection is more valuable than ever for Matthew Stafford, Rams
item.description: Los Angeles is in trouble if it can’t keep its quarterback upright
item.content:encoded:
Matthew Stafford did not have his finest game against the Denver Broncos.

It wasn’t a complete disaster by any means for the reigning NFL MVP in Week 3. He completed a subpar 54.5% of his passes for a gaudy 390 yards and a pair of touchdowns, but it took him 55 attempts to get there and he also threw a pair of interceptions, both of which came in the fourth quarter (one of which was returned for a touchdown, one of which was on the final snap of the game).

When you dive into the advanced numbers, it’s more of the same. In the loss, Stafford posted just .03 EPA/play, a success rate of just 43% and -0.1 completion percentage over expectation (all according to RBSDM.com).

Through three weeks, Stafford’s PFF grade is a flat 60.0, dead-on average by their grading scale. Now, PFF’s grading has always been flawed and is especially unreliable now given what that company has gone through in the last year, but a middling grade at least somewhat matches the eye test through three games.

There is one distinct and easy-to-grasp area in which the Rams and their star quarterback are struggling mightily, and it came to a head against the Broncos: pressure.

According to Next Gen Stats, when under pressure on Sunday night, Stafford was just 5-of-18 passing for 61 yards with the first interception of the night and he was also sacked four times. From a clean pocket, his fortunes couldn’t have been farther in the opposite direction, save for one play. He went 25-of-35 when kept clean, throwing for 329 yards and two touchdowns plus the desperation pick to close the game.

That’s 3.4 yards per attempt while under pressure, 9.4 yards per attempt from a clean pocket. It’s easy to understand why that is so devastating to an offense.

Obviously, no quarterback in the NFL is ever going to be free from pressure on every snap throughout a game, let alone a season. You have to deal with pressure constantly, especially going up against the league’s best defenses (a group you can still consider the Broncos to be included in). But when the disparity in success is that enormous, it puts even more emphasis on holding the line for your quarterback.

Things were even more stark in the second half when Denver made its comeback. The Broncos pressured Stafford on 57.7% of his second-half dropbacks this weekend, compared to just 23.5% in the first half (again from Next Gen Stats).

It goes without saying that this is something the Rams have to clean up going forward. Concerningly, this has been a trend through the first sixth of this season. Against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 1, Stafford was pressured on 44% of his dropbacks, the highest pressure rate he had faced since Dec. 2024. No one is going to tell you the offense was spectacular or even good in the opener, and no one is going to tell you they were impressed by the offense in the second half of Week 3.

Against the Giants in Week 2, by the way, Stafford only faced pressure on five dropbacks and torched that defense.

The offensive line was one area that drew some concern, or at least some sideways glances, leading into the season. There’s time to improve and it’s not like they’re wholly lacking talent. But this is a legitimate concern and one that needs to be fixed as quickly as possible. With an aging quarterback who’s not exactly fleet of foot, keeping him upright needs to be addressed urgently.

It’s too early to throw in the towel on this team, even at 1-2. That should be a given. But if there’s anything that can derail a title-contending season, your quarterback falling under constant siege and suffering the consequences of it would be at the top of the list.

item.title: Mike Vrabel: Drake Maye needs to "relax"
item.description: A year after finishing second in the NFL MVP voting, Patriots quarterback Drake Maye won't have to worry about nearly missing out on the award in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
A year after finishing second in the NFL MVP voting, Patriots quarterback Drake Maye won't have to worry about nearly missing out on the award in 2026.

Through three games of the the third season his career, Maye has regressed. Badly.

Last year, he had 31 touchdown passes and eight interceptions. This year, he has one touchdown pass and six interceptions. His passer rating has plummeted from 113.5 to 58.6.

Sunday's 35-6 disaster in Duval included three turnovers and no touchdowns.

Appearing Monday on WEEI's The Greg Hill Show, coach Mike Vrabel was asked about Maye's obvious issues with decision-making.

“I think quarterbacks want to make plays," Vrabel said, via Mike Reiss of ESPN. "I think they want to throw touchdowns. I think sometimes when Greg and I go golfing, we really want to make a good score, right? Sometimes we’re so focused on it, we try to choke the life out of the golf club, and we’re squeezing it so damn tight that the ball has no choice but to go sideways. We need to stop trying to choke the life out of every single play. We need to relax. We need to settle in and go play football and not try to force things that aren’t there.”

It seems at this point to be more than bad decisions. Simms explained on Monday's PFT Live that Maye has developed mechanical flaws, including a flicking of the wrist before the makes his throws. Also, Simms believes Maye is trying too hard to guide his throws, in lieu of letting it rip.

If the Patriots agree with the assessment, it won't be easy to coach these things out of Maye during football season, when there's a fresh train always heading down the tracks. And the next stop is Buffalo.

Last year in Week 5, Maye led the Patriots to a win in their final game at the Bills' old stadium. This year in Week 4, Maye has a chance to reverse a troubling trend that has become a full-blown narrative.

item.title: Mekhi Becton signs with Packers
item.description: Former Eagles guard finds another new NFL home.
item.content:encoded:
In light of the Philadelphia Eagles’ interior offensive line struggles, some have wondered if the team might be interested in bringing Mekhi Becton back to Philly.

There have been calls for a reunion from some community members here at Bleeding Green Nation:

Becton is no longer a free agent after signing to the Green Bay Packers’ practice squad on Monday morning, according to a report from NFL insider Jeremy Fowler. Becton also reportedly drew interest from the Pittsburgh Steelers. No word of any interest from the Eagles, who currently still have an open roster spot.

There was reporting on the Eagles’ lack of interest in Becton earlier this year from Tony Pauline:

“During Shrine Bowl week, I was told that Becton has returned to many of his former ways, including firing the agency that helped get his game back on track, and that has raised red flags with the Philadelphia Eagles. The Eagles were surprised (if not shocked) and disappointed by the turn of events.“

Becton’s career has taken a turn for the worse ever since his Super Bowl LIX success. After the 2024 season, he left Philly to sign with the Los Angeles Chargers in free agency. Becton struggled and got benched while the Bolts fielded one of the worst offensive lines in the NFL. Becton was cut by the Chargers after 2025 and remained available as a free agent until joining the Packers, who are in desperate need of offensive line help.

If the Eagles felt like Becton was part of the solution moving forward, they would’ve made a better effort to bring him back.

item.title: Fins Up, Fins Down | Winners and losers from Miami Dolphins week three loss
item.description: Chris Bell takes over lead receiver duties while Miami loses De’Von Achane to knee injury.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins showed signs of life against the Kansas City Chiefs — keeping the deficit to just one score until a late touchdown pass from Patrick Mahomes to Travis Kelce sealed their fate. Unfortunately, “keeping it close” doesn’t amount to a hill of beans in the win/loss column. However, like head coach Jeff Hafley has preached since he took the job in Miami, this year isn’t necessarily about winning or losing — it’s about showing growth, building a solid foundation and getting better every time the team takes the field.

I believe they did that against the Chiefs.

So, whose stock is up and whose stock is down after week three’s loss to Kansas City?

FINS UP

Our Fins Up player from Miami’s week three loss is rookie receiver Chris Bell. Fellow standout rookie Caleb Douglas sat out this week’s game due to an ankle injury, giving Bell an opportunity to shine. He did just that — nabbing four receptions for a team leading 67 yards receiving — nearly 1/3 of quarterback Malik Willis’ 210 yards passing.

Bell’s quick return to action following a late-season ACL tear last November while playing in college at Louisville is nothing short of astounding. He’s shown flashes of the player who was talked about as a late first-round selection in the 2026 NFL Draft prior to his knee injury, and as he continues to work his way back to full strength, the Dolphins will continue to benefit from his solid play.

I don’t think we’re too far away from Bell’s first touchdown grab as a member of the Miami Dolphins. Can he find paydirt this weekend against the Minnesota Vikings? Stay tuned!

FINS DOWN

Through no fault of his own, running back De’Von Achane earns this week’s Fins Down designation. On just his third carry of the game against Kansas City, Miami’s electric running back went down with a seemingly innocuous knee injury. Unfortunately, it was anything but.

Achane wouldn’t return to the game — further hampering Miami’s already wounded rushing attack. The Dolphins would amass just 46 yards rushing from players not named Achane or Malik Willis for the rest of the tilt against the Chiefs.

Following the loss, Hafley said the early outlooks regarding Achane’s knee “do not sound very optimistic.” Those are not the words any Dolphins’ fan wants to hear when it comes to the team’s most dangerous weapon.

item.title: 5 key plays that led to the Cowboys loss
item.description: What was the worst moment for the Cowboys in your opinion?
item.content:encoded:
Whether you blame personnel, injuries, or the field conditions at Maracanã Stadium, the Dallas Cowboys’ defense struggled to contain the Baltimore Ravens. Rookies Caleb Downs and Jaishawn Barham offered some bright spots, but those flashes weren’t consistent enough to win.

On the other side, the Cowboys offense blew opportunities in the redzone through poor execution and play-calling, while other mistakes plagued them between the 20s.

The loss drops Dallas to 1-2 with plenty still to address. The team has a long flight home to begin sorting it out. Here are the five critical plays that sealed a gut-wrenching defeat in Brazil.

Lamar Jackson’s 21-yard run

The defensive collapse was foreshadowed early in the first quarter. After Dallas took a 10-0 lead, there was hope the Cowboys could keep the pressure on and force Baltimore into one-dimensional football. That never happened.

The lid came off right after Brandon Aubrey’s kickoff—one of two he sent out of bounds, both of which gifted the Ravens strong starting field position. Facing 1st-and-15, Lamar Jackson got around the edge on a zone-read with an escort block from Mark Andrews.

From that point, Baltimore used misdirection in the run game to create lanes and throwing windows while exposing the Cowboys’ eye discipline at the second level. The drive ended with a wildcat touchdown run by Derrick Henry, and many more points followed for the Ravens.

49-yard penalty on Markquese Bell

Penalties repeatedly altered the game’s complexion—some questionable, others clear. Clinging to a three-point lead, the Cowboys had a chance to force Baltimore behind the sticks. Instead, Lamar Jackson scrambled free and threw a slightly underthrown pass toward Devontez Walker. Markquese Bell arrived early in coverage and made illegal contact, drawing a massive 49-yard pass-interference flag.

It was the second such call of the drive (the first, on DaRon Bland, was highly debatable). Bell’s penalty proved especially costly as Derrick Henry scored on the next play.

Terence Steele’s hold takes away the first down

Dallas caught a tough break when a Jake Ferguson reception was ruled a fumble even though replay suggested he never had full control. Desperate to stop the bleeding, the Cowboys forced a stop on the ensuing Ravens possession. The offense was finally gaining traction.

On a critical 3rd-and-9, Dak Prescott appeared to hit George Pickens for a 20-yard gain—until a Terence Steele holding penalty wiped it out. Forced into a long field-goal try, Brandon Aubrey’s 59-yard attempt was blocked by Keondre Jackson, one of several special-teams miscues on the day. How much Steele contributed to the blocked kick remains unclear, but the sequence was painful for the veteran tackle.

Schoonmaker’s false start changes the play sheet

Dallas did a solid job managing the clock to set up one final possession in regulation. When CeeDee Lamb drew a pass-interference call at the two-yard line with 23 seconds left, the entire playbook opened up.

The Cowboys went aggressive with a fade to George Pickens that fell incomplete. On second down they could have handed the ball to Javonte Williams, who had run effectively all night. Instead, Luke Schoonmaker’s false start removed all doubt. Those five costly yards forced Dallas into a throw-only situation, handed Baltimore breathing room, and set up the final sequence.

Ran out of bodies

Failing to score the go-ahead touchdown on that last drive was disappointing. What no one expected was the defense completely disintegrating and allowing easy access to field-goal range.

Already depleted after losing multiple safeties and then watching Shavon Revel exit with a knee injury, the Cowboys generated no pressure on Lamar Jackson. He had all day to find Zay Flowers open for the 27-yard gain that set up Tyler Loop’s 56-yard game-winner. Jackson called timeout with one second remaining, and Loop delivered the dagger.

Think about the agonizing losses in Cowboys history—Jared Cook’s toe-drag, Matt Stafford’s fake spike into a quarterback sneak. This one ranks among the worst in the last 15 years, with injuries taking center stage at the bitter end. This one is going to hurt for a while.

item.title: Giants-Titans: 5 plays that led to the Giants’ Week 3 victory
item.description: Five plays, or sequence of plays, that led to the Giants’ 12-7 win.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants improved to 2-1 after their 12-7 victory in the rainy conditions at MetLife Stadium on Sunday. The Giants’ special teams helped secure the win, with Jordan Stout averaging 53 yards on five punts and rookie kicker Dominic Zvada booting all four of his attempts for the 12 points the Jameis Winston-led offense scored. Winston didn’t prove he should be the Giants’ quarterback for the rest of the season, but he did enough to secure the win.

The Giants possessed the football for nine more minutes than the Titans, and the Giants were penalized ten times for 88 yards. The Titans ended up outgaining the Giants 262 yards to 238. Both offenses were inefficient on third down; the Giants went 4 of 13 and the Titans 5 of 13 — all five in the second half.

Arvell Reese led the Giants with 12 tackles, with Dru Phillips recording 11 and Tremaine Edmunds recording 10. However, the vaunted Giants’ pass rush lost Brian Burns midway through the game to a right knee injury, and the Giants did not sack Ward once in the game. The defense bent badly in the second half after a hot start. It’s something to monitor moving forward. The Giants were lucky enough to escape with a win against the Titans, and here are five plays that were crucial for one reason or another.

Play 1: Jevon Holland!

Holland has an interception in each game so far this season — none bigger than this game-sealing pick:

Holland’s patience and vision were exceptional on this play against the second-year signal caller. Holland started to close width on Ward, who was scrambling to the boundary, but the safety read the quarterback’s eyes and sank underneath the route breaking behind him. Holland intercepted the pass and secured the Giants’ second win of the season. Holland is having a fantastic season for the Giants.

Play(s) 2: FIVE three-and-outs to start

Brian Daboll’s return did not go as planned in the rainy, windy conditions of East Rutherford, N.J. New York’s defense shut down Tennessee’s rushing attack, holding them to 13 first-half rushing yards, an average of 2.2 yards per carry. The first Tennessee drives resulted in three-and-outs, resulting in 32 total yards. Wan’Dale Robinson failed to secure two catchable passes, and the offense struggled to do anything against the Giants until the two-minute drill.

The Titans did respond well in the second half. Brian Daboll started attacking the Giants on quick out routes, which allowed Cam Ward to get into a rhythm. The Titans finished the day with a twelve-play drive and two thirteen-play drives. Unfortunately, for Tennessee, it resulted in just one touchdown and the aformentioned Jevon Holland — game-sealing — interception.

Play 3: 59-yard field goal try

Tennessee drove the football to the Giants’ 41-yard line, and Robert Saleh opted to kick a 59-yard field goal, down 6-0. Joey Slye missed the kick, and the Giants took over with 41 seconds left in the first half. Jameis Winston threw two incompletions and then found Malik Nabers on a quick slant that converted the third-and-10. He then found Darnell Mooney for 7yards to help set up Dominic Zvada’s third field goal, a 39-yarder that gave the Giants a two-possession lead. 

Play(s) 4: Fourth-down stop

The Titans had a 12-play, 62-yard drive that yielded zero points after Cam Ward sailed this ball incomplete. The Giants’ defense bent through the drive, surrendered a 20-yard completion to Carnell Tate and a 12-yard run by Tony Pollard. Still, the Giants defense clamped down with deceptive pressure looks in the red area that resulted in two incomplete passes. Ward missed an open Tate in the end zone on the third-and-goal play. 

Play 5: Cam Skattebo the receiver 

Points were hard to come by in this sloppy, weathered game, but the Giants broke the 0-0 tie after this third-and-seven conversion by Jameis Winston to running back Cam Skattebo. Matt Nagy called a familiar 3×1 look with the pivot/corner to the three-receiver side and the running back releasing toward the lone receiver side; Skattebo does a great job extending his route downfield, and Winston took a SHOT as he released to the open back. In patented fashion, Skattebo finishes the play with tenacity.

item.title: Packers keep adding veteran offensive linemen by signing Mekhi Becton
item.description: Becton joins former teammate Laken Tomlinson with the Packers.
item.content:encoded:
At least this can be said for the Green Bay Packers’ front office: they are trying to do something to address the team’s issues on the offensive line. A few days after signing former Pro Bowl guard Laken Tomlinson off the Dallas Cowboys’ practice squad over the weekend, the Packers are adding another former first-round draft pick to the roster.

Joining Tomlinson in Green Bay will be Mekhi Becton, a six-year NFL veteran and the 11th overall pick in the 2020 NFL Draft out of the University of Louisville. Jeremy Fowler of ESPN reported that Becton worked out for the Packers on Monday morning and then signed with the team almost immediately.

Becton has been a primary starter for three different teams over the last three years, spending 2025 with the Los Angeles Chargers after starting at right guard for the Super Bowl-winning Philadelphia Eagles during the 2024 season. He started his career with the New York Jets, but he missed almost all of the 2021 season with a torn ACL. He then injured the same knee in training camp the following season and missed the entirety of the 2022 campaign before returning to play 16 games in 2023.

With the Chargers, Becton struggled a bit, but he played 16 of the team’s possible 18 games with 15 starts, all at right guard. Becton also played against the Packers twice as an Eagle in 2024, playing every snap at right guard in the Eagles’ Week 1 and Wild Card victories. The 6-foot-7, 360-pounder becomes a real candidate to step in and get immediate playing time, possibly competing with Tomlinson for snaps at guard.

Interestingly, Becton and Tomlinson overlapped as teammates with the Jets for two seasons, during the 2022 and 2023 seasons. As noted earlier, Becton missed the entire 2022 campaign, but the two started at left tackle and left guard, respectively, during the 2023 season. Also involved in the Jets’ organization that year were a slew of former Packers: former Green Bay offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett held the OC and playcalling duties in New York, while wide receivers Allen Lazard, Randall Cobb, and Malik Taylor and quarterback Tim Boyle were on that team as well. There was one other notable former Packer on the Jets’ roster that year: 2023 was the year that the Packers traded Aaron Rodgers to the Jets as well, though his season ended just a few plays into Week 1 when he tore his Achilles tendon.

The signings of both players will likely appear on the NFL’s transaction wire on Monday afternoon. Expect the Packers to make room for these two players on the 53-man roster by placing Zach Bako-Bewele and Jayden Reed on injured reserve.

item.title: Titans vs. Ravens odds: Opening lines for Week 4 matchup
item.description: The Titans are double-digit underdogs again
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans have opened as an 11.5-point road underdog against the Baltimore Ravens in Week 4 at FanDuel Sportsbook. 11.5 isn’t enough. For me to put any actual money on the Titans in this match-up, the line would need to be closer to +17.5.

It seems like every week there has been a storyline surrounding the game. In Week 1, it was Robert Saleh facing his old team, the New York Jets. In Week 3, it was Brian Daboll and half of the Titans’ coaching staff and roster facing off against Daboll’s former team, the New York Giants. This week, the Titans face off against Derrick Henry for the first time since he joined the Baltimore Ravens.

If the Titans are ever going to win a game, they are going to have to get some consistency from the offense. They can’t get consistency from the offense until they get consistency from Cam Ward. We have yet to see that through the first 20 games of his NFL career. That doesn’t mean it can never happen, but it sure would be nice to see signs of progress.

item.title: Dexter Lawrence: Our goal wasn't to go undefeated, we'll own this one
item.description: Through two games, the Bengals’ defense looked like it had undergone a significant transformation in the offseason — partially due to the addition of Dexter Lawrence.
item.content:encoded:
Through two games, the Bengals’ defense looked like it had undergone a significant transformation in the offseason — partially due to the addition of Dexter Lawrence.

But then came Sunday’s divisional matchup against the Steelers, with Pittsburgh’s offense generating 411 yards — including 138 on the ground — en route to defeating Cincinnati 30-27.

Lawrence, in his eighth pro season, provided some perspective after the game.

“I think it's a reminder to show y'all that we’re not going to go undefeated,” Lawrence said, via Jay Morrison of SI.com. “No year is gonna be perfect. … Our goal wasn’t to go undefeated. So we’ll own this one. We'll come back next week and go out there and play.”

Lawrence added that Sunday’s performance “wasn’t us.”

“We know we can't allow that; however it comes, however they try to do it,” Lawrence said. “We made a lot of mistakes, and that's what kept the game close and then ultimately helped them win.

“A lot of what was going on was self-inflicted. … You watched the game. You know what happened. I don't think it was anything special that they had going on. We just didn't do well on our end.”

The Bengals will get another tough opponent next week when the Jaguars come to Cincinnati.

item.title: Ravens' Tyler Loop lost his helmet before game-winning field goal, Ronaldo-style celebration
item.description: Ravens kicker Tyler Loop had a lot to figure out in a short amount of time. It worked out pretty well.
item.content:encoded:
Baltimore Ravens kicker Tyler Loop had a lot going through his mind in a short amount of time prior to his game-winning field goal on Sunday.

After the Dallas Cowboys tied the game with seven seconds remaining, Lamar Jackson hit Zay Flowers on a 27-yard reception. The Ravens' miraculously had a chance to win Sunday's game in Rio after it appeared the game was destined for overtime.

The problem? Loop was missing his hat.

"I couldn't find my helmet," Loop explained to Ravens teammate Marlon Humphrey after the game.

The @tyler_loop exclusive with @marlon_humphrey 😂😂😂 pic.twitter.com/a6YOKvDKnz

— Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) September 28, 2026

"Oh my gosh," Humphrey said, "so it didn't even almost happen."

Loop explained that from the time Jackson signaled timeout to when he needed to start trotting on the field, he had around 15 seconds to find his helmet. No pressure.

On top of that, Loop hadn't even been warming up on the sideline. He didn't expect to even have a kick to attempt before OT.

When asked whether the lack of a helmet or warmup time rattled him, Loop shrugged and said his attitude in the moment was: "F it, we ball."

He balled, all right. Loop found his helmet and made the kick, tucking it just inside the left upright with plenty of length to spare. The 56-yarder was the second-longest field goal of his career and sent the Ravens home winners in an instant classic. It was a terrific ending for the kicker whose Week 18 miss at the end of regulation kept the Ravens out of the playoffs last season.

But there was one more matter to handle: the celebration.

Ravens punter Ryan Eckley earlier had suggested a soccer-style knee slide if Loop hit a game winner, given that they were in Brazil. Loop immediately nixed the idea. He knew that even for the greatest footballers in the world, it can be a perilous endeavor.

Mbappé tries to knee slide on the grass and fails pic.twitter.com/nQrsAp914y

— mia´s media acc (@panqsinpasas) September 22, 2026

But Loop still wanted the soccer homage in some form. In the moment, he gave Rio de Janeiro and Maracanã Stadium something to remember — a Ronaldo-style "Siuuu!" celebration. The crowd absolutely ate it up.

"When in Brazil, man," Loop said. "When in Brazil …"

For good measure, here's the radio call in Portuguese:

TYLER LOOP COM O FIELD GOAL DA VITÓRIAAAAAA! 🤯🤯

RAVENS VENCEM O PRIMEIRO NFL RIO GAME DA HISTÓRIA! 🇧🇷

📺: #BALvsDAL ao vivo no @sportv e GETV pic.twitter.com/S7wYcMVg9q

— NFL Brasil (@NFLBrasil) September 27, 2026

That's a lot of action to pack into about one minute — all unscripted, too. There's a saying in Brazil that fits well: "Quem não tem cão, caça com gato." It literally means: Who doesn't have a dog hunts with a cat.

Loop had no warmup, no helmet and no celebration figured out. He just locked in, made the kick and let everything else take care of itself. It worked out pretty well.
